title: The Colonial Architecture of AI: Platform Capitalism, Digital Taylorism, and Contested Labour in the Global South

detail.title: The Colonial Architecture of AI: Platform Capitalism, Digital Taylorism, and Contested Labour in the Global South

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Head of IT & Security at meldCX, an Australian AI software company. This professional position provided practical insight into AI supply chain governance challenges but did not influence the research design, analysis, or conclusions. This research was conducted independently in the author's own time. No financial or other material interests exist that could be perceived as influencing the objectivity of this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research involved analysis of publicly available secondary sources (academic literature, investigative journalism, litigation records, and worker-built tools). No primary data collection with human subjects was conducted. Therefore, formal ethics review and approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This article challenges the prevailing narrative of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as autonomous technology, demonstrating that AI's functionality depends on a hidden global workforce engaged in "ghost work" (Gray & Suri, 2019). Drawing on labour process theory, post-colonial critique, and platform capitalism studies, we synthesise evidence from investigative journalism, litigation records, and worker organising to map the integrated architecture structuring AI's human infrastructure. We demonstrate that Platform Capitalism provides the economic imperative for large-scale labour extraction (Section 2), Digital Colonialism structures this extraction geographically around Global South exploitation (Section 2), and Digital Taylorism provides the algorithmic control mechanism managing fragmented workers (Section 3). Critically, this architecture generates contested terrain (Section 4): platforms manufacture consent through gamification, yet this consent is structurally fragile, collapsing when exploitation becomes too blatant. When consent fails, workers develop algorithmic counter-power-using technology to surveil capital through tools like Turkopticon and mutual aid networks. We analyse three alternative models-decolonial AI, participatory design, and platform cooperativism-demonstrating that all confront the same structural barrier: market competition systematically selects against ethical practice (Section 5). We argue that architectural opacity is economically necessary under platform capitalism, not incidental, and that meaningful AI governance requires system-level transformation addressing labour exploitation as constitutive of AI development. AI ethics must be reconceptualised as global labour justice.

title: Analyzing the Resilience of Mnemonic Passwords Against AI-Powered Brute-Force Attacks
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Analyzing the Resilience of Mnemonic Passwords Against AI-Powered Brute-Force Attacks
detail.abstract: In this research was conducted a comprehensive study on the resilience of mnemonic passwords to modern AI attacks. We analyzed five main mnemonic passwords generation methods, which are SenSub-sentence substitution, KbCg-keyboard layout modification, UsForm-mathematical formulas, Splns-special character insertion, and Alphapwd-letter-shape-based generation. For testing, we used a generative adversarial network trained on real user passwords. The results have shown that, mnemonic passwords when they are used correctly demonstrate high resistance to AI attacks as none of the 677 test passwords were cracked after 20 000 attempts. The most effective, difficult to crack, and possessing good memorability methods (87-91% success rate) have turned out to be SenSub and Alphapwd. However, the ones that were found to be vulnerable to targeted attacks are KbCg and UsForm due to their limited search space and dependence on a base passwords. In this study, we confirmed that mnemonic passwords can serve as a compromise between convenience and security, but the effectiveness of mnemonic passwords directly depends on user literacy in applying these methods. In order to counter future AI threats, we have to combine multiple generation methods, use long phrases, regularly update the transformation rules, and also combine strong mnemonic passwords with two-factor authentication in critical needs.

title: Artificially Translating the Law: Risks of Decentering the Human Expert
affiliations: University of New Brunswick Faculty of Law and Independent Researcher

detail.title: Artificially Translating the Law: Risks of Decentering the Human Expert
detail.abstract: This article examines the growing use of artificial translation in legal settings, highlighting the significant risks and costs it entails. These risks include reduced reliability, breaches of privacy and confidentiality, copyright violations, algorithmic bias, and threats to access to justice. Together, they pose both immediate and long-term costs to the legal system, which legal professionals have largely overlooked. The article also identifies a contradiction in how institutions approach this issue: while publicly affirming the value of human translators and interpreters, governments and courts increasingly fund technological solutions developed without their input. This disconnect has led to frustration and attrition among legal language professionals, deepening the shortage of qualified experts. For these reasons the article argues that sidelining human expertise is a misguided and dangerous trend and makes a strong case for keeping human professionals central to legal translation and interpretation.

title: Smart Contracts and AI-Driven ADR In Nigeria: Are we Legally Ready?
affiliations: Joseph Ayo Babalola University (JABU) and University of Nigeria

detail.title: Smart Contracts and AI-Driven ADR In Nigeria: Are we Legally Ready?
detail.abstract: This paper critically assesses Nigeria’s legal and regulatory preparedness for the adoption of smart contracts and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms. It examines how existing laws accommodate automation, machine-based decision-making, and algorithmic dispute resolution. Drawing on key Nigerian legislation, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, the Cybercrimes Act (as amended) 2024, the Evidence Act 2011 (as amended) 2023, the Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023, and the Investment and Securities Act 2025, and the UNCITRAL Model Law on Automated Contracting (2024), the paper explores critical issues of enforceability, liability, data privacy, evidentiary standards, and regulatory oversight. While the UNCITRAL Model Law legally recognizes actions by automated systems and contracts in computer code, and Nigerian laws like the NDP Act provide for data protection and the Evidence Act for electronic evidence, the paper argues that Nigeria, despite a foundational legal framework, faces doctrinal and operational gaps. These include challenges concerning the binding force of self-executing clauses (akin to contracts in computer code), limitations on fully autonomous AI decisions (as hinted by the NDP Act's automated decision-making provisions), and the risk of regulatory fragmentation among diverse oversight bodies. The paper concludes with recommendations for legal reform, institutional coordination, and rights-based safeguards to align Nigeria’s legal system with AIpowered legal technologies.

title: Competition and Regulation of Cloud Computing Services: Economic Analysis and Review of EU Policies
affiliations: University of Siena and University of Regensburg

detail.title: Competition and Regulation of Cloud Computing Services: Economic Analysis and Review of EU Policies
detail.abstract: Cloud infrastructures and services have become key building blocks of the digital society. As more businesses and organizations migrate their infrastructure and services to the cloud, the cloud industry is rapidly growing and has by now become a key enabler of digital businesses and a vital infrastructure for the economy as a whole. At the same time, the digital technologies that enable cloud infrastructures and services are constantly evolving, thus facilitating the development of new cloud services, most notably in the areas of artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things. This research report takes stock of the recent developments and major policy updates in the EU with a focus on competition and the proper functioning of markets in the cloud computing industry. To this end, the report provides a coordinated legal review and analysis of the recent policy initiatives as well as an economic analysis of the competition issues that arise with regard to the peculiar economic and technical characteristics of cloud computing. In this vein, the report provides an economic and legal assessment of the recently adopted policies and regulations as well as their justifications from an economic perspective. Furthermore, the report contributes to the ongoing and future policy process by informing the interpretation and implementation of already adopted policies as well as decisions on further policies and interventions.

title: Cross-Cutting Issues for DSA Systemic Risk Management: An Agenda for Cooperation
affiliations: University of East Anglia, University of Regensburg, UCL School of Management, University College London and University of East Anglia (UEA) - Centre for Competition Policy

detail.title: Cross-Cutting Issues for DSA Systemic Risk Management: An Agenda for Cooperation
detail.abstract: In August 2023, the providers of the first 19 services to be designated as very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) under the Digital Services Act (DSA) submitted their first assessments of systemic risks stemming from the services. While the European Commission and the service providers are understandably focused on compliance, in this paper we argue that the Digital Services Board, researchers, civil society groups, and others can be looking across services and risk areas to understand what the most pressing sources of systemic risk are, where common vulnerabilities arise, and what mitigations effectively reduce negative effects. Systemic risk assessment is an annual requirement, and we can expect a cycle of continual learning leading, ideally, to improvements in the prevention of harm and adaptation to changes in services and user behaviour. This paper sets out issues that we find cut across individual designated services and, we argue, that should be key areas for analysis across services, especially ones of similar type, as part of that process. This paper therefore speaks to the Commission and the Board, as regulators with their overarching view and information gathering powers, and also lays out a research agenda for academics and others who intend to contribute to the management of systemic risk in practice and to wider debates about the governance of digital services.

title: Effective Implementation of Requirements for High-Risk AI Systems Under the AI Act: Transparency and Appropriate Accuracy
affiliations: University of Regensburg

detail.title: Effective Implementation of Requirements for High-Risk AI Systems Under the AI Act: Transparency and Appropriate Accuracy
detail.abstract:
This paper takes a first step toward analysing and deriving recommendations for the efficient and effective operationalisation of selected requirements under the European AI Act (AIA). The paper identifies open questions about the implementation of provisions for high-risk AI systems, evaluates potential approaches to address these questions in light of the underlying trade-offs, and proposes further steps to establish actionable guidance for providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems. The analysis focuses specifically on the transparency provisions in Art. 13 AIA and the provisions on appropriate accuracy in Art. 15 AIA for high-risk AI systems.

A central challenge to the implementation of the AIA lies in its broad scope. Given the wide range of technical approaches employed in high-risk AI systems and the diverse use cases to which they are applied, deriving general yet useful and appropriate criteria is inherently difficult. To address this challenge, the paper proposes elements and principles that could be established at the general level of the AIA to promote consistency across risk domains and applications. These recommendations include defining main categories of information to be provided under the transparency requirement and establishing a general principle for determining the appropriate level of accuracy of high-risk AI systems. Furthermore, the paper highlights requirements and specifications that demand more granular guidance, such as within specific risk domains, to ensure effectiveness and proportionality. For example, this includes criteria to determine whether the interpretability of a high-risk AI system’s outputs requires using intrinsically interpretable models or post-hoc interpretation techniques, as well as guidance on what performance dimensions constitute relevant accuracy criteria for a given high-risk AI system.

detail.abstract: The explosive rise and rapid decline of the NFT art market has intensified uncertainty over whether an NFT constitutes a security subject to regulation by the SEC. In the absence of clear rulemaking, the SEC has relied heavily on regulation-by-enforcement, producing inconsistent guidance and prompting widespread concern among NFT creators. This Article provides the most comprehensive examination to date of the legal landscape governing NFT art. It traces the evolution of blockchain-based digital art; analyzes major SEC enforcement actions; assesses artists’ attempts to obtain declaratory relief; and evaluates the significance of the landmark Adonis v. Yuga Labs decision, which rejected securities classification for certain NFTs under the Howey test. The Article further surveys pending legislative proposals—including the NFT Act, the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, and the Responsible Financial Innovation Act—and highlights the growing role of no-action letters following the SEC’s 2025 DoubleZero determination. Finally, it explores how the second Trump Administration’s deregulatory stance is reshaping the SEC’s approach to digital assets. Synthesizing these developments, the Article proposes a practical framework for NFT artists to structure, market, and sell their works without triggering securities regulation, emphasizing economic-reality analysis, limitations on pooling and promotional claims, and strategic use of no-action relief.

title: Security and Privacy Testing in Mental Health Applications: An Empirical Study on Vulnerabilities and Protection Gaps
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, and Karlstad University

detail.title: Security and Privacy Testing in Mental Health Applications: An Empirical Study on Vulnerabilities and Protection Gaps
detail.abstract: Context: Mobile applications (apps) in the mental health domain handle highly sensitive personal data, making security and privacy essential quality attributes. Problem: However, studies have shown that many of these apps fail to implement proper safeguards, potentially exposing users to serious risks. Objective: This paper presents an empirical study focused on identifying security and privacy vulnerabilities in mental health apps through systematic testing. Method: We selected a sample of mental health-related apps and conducted a series of security tests based on recognized best practices and guidelines, secure coding, data exposure, server security, authentication flaws, readability of privacy policies, and privacy misconfigurations. The analysis revealed recurring weaknesses, including insufficient encryption, poor session management, and inadequate privacy policies. Our findings underscore the need for integrating security and privacy testing into the development cycle of health-related systems, particularly those involving mental health. The study contributes to the field by identifying critical gaps and providing recommendations for enhancing the robustness of such apps.

detail.abstract: In an era where artificial intelligence (AI) is seamlessly integrated into daily life, our paper investigates the intersection of generative AI and cybersecurity, exploring how AI platforms like ChatGPT, Dall-E, and Midjourney, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs), along with the Big Five personality traits, influence individual self-worth. We interrogate AI's capacity to meet human needs as outlined by Maslow's hierarchy of needs and its simultaneous potential to pose cybersecurity risks—especially privacy infringements and psychological manipulation. Our findings highlight significant cybersecurity challenges, including vulnerability to data breaches and exploiting personality traits, which can undermine human worth. By presenting an innovative model that marries Maslow's hierarchy with the Big Five traits, the study underscores the critical role of cybersecurity in the ethical integration of AI into society. We call for a proactive balance in AI advancement that prioritizes robust cybersecurity strategies to protect and elevate human dignity in the digital age.

keywords: Content moderation recommender systems. License: CC-BY-NC-SA

publicationDetails.detailsText: Erasmus Law Review, volume 18, issue 1, 2025[10.5553/ELR.000291]

detail.abstract: By recognising the pivotal role of the internet in shaping public discourse, this article embarks on a critical evaluation of the existing regulatory frameworks, aiming to navigate the challenges introduced by the symbiotic relationship between digital platforms' algorithms and critically assessing the efficacy of current regulatory approaches in preserving freedom of expression. First, this article meticulously examines four challenges: algorithmic biases, automated content moderation, transparency and accountability of algorithms, and intermediaries intertwined with algorithms, scrutinising their role in enabling filter bubbles and echo chambers. Second, we examine the regulatory landscape concerning freedom of expression on digital platforms through the lenses of critical instruments such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the E-Commerce Directive (ECD) and then the recently introduced Digital Services Act (DSA). A normative analysis of the DSA in light of its challenges to uphold freedom of expression, compared with its predecessors, reveals the evolution of legal frameworks in response to the dynamic digital environment. Although legally designated as hosting services, Very Large Online Platforms' (VLOPs) use of tracking technologies, algorithmic content curation and behavioural profiling places them beyond the passive or neutral roles envisioned for hosts or mere conduits. This hybrid operational model exposes a critical structural incoherence within the DSA's tripartite framework, which risks leaving the most powerful digital actors insufficiently regulated. Finally, the synthesis crystallises the articles' findings, emphasising the imperativeness of enhanced transparency, independent regulatory oversight, and the imperative to decouple regulatory financing from and by the big tech.

title: Trade Execution Flow as the Underlying Source of Market Dynamics
affiliations: Lomonosov  Moscow State University - Faculty of Mechanics and Mathematics, Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic University, Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic University, Ioffe Institute, Ioffe Institute and Ioffe Institute

detail.title: Trade Execution Flow as the Underlying Source of Market Dynamics
detail.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate experimentally that the execution flow, I=dV/dt, is the fundamental driving force of market dynamics. We develop a numerical framework to calculate execution flow from sampled moments using the Radon-Nikodym derivative. A notable feature of this approach is its ability to automatically determine thresholds that can serve as actionable triggers. The technique also determines the characteristic time scale directly from the corresponding eigenproblem. The methodology has been validated on actual market data to support these findings. Additionally, we introduce a framework based on the Christoffel function spectrum, which is invariant under arbitrary non-degenerate linear transformations of input attributes and offers an alternative to traditional principal component analysis (PCA), which is limited to unitary invariance.

title: Ternary Logic (TL): Evidentiary Framework for Economic Systems

detail.title: Ternary Logic (TL): Evidentiary Framework for Economic Systems
detail.abstract: Modern economic infrastructures, strained by volatility and algorithmic speed, remain confined to the limits of bivalent logic. The binary divide between true/false and act/inaction amplifies systemic risk-manifesting in flash crashes, supply-chain disruptions, and unstable policy reactions. Ternary Logic (TL) introduces a third computational state: the Epistemic Hold, that enables a structured, auditable pause when data proves insufficient or contradictory. This converts hesitation from a liability into a measurable instrument of intelligent uncertainty management. Evolving from Ternary Moral Logic (TML), TL retains its technical architecture: immutable ledgers, verifiable provenance, and triadic decision dynamics, while translating them from moral judgment to evidentiary integrity. At its core stands the Goukassian Principle, preserving continuity between conscience and accountability. Its protection is ensured by the Hybrid Shield, a multilayered defense combining cryptographic anchoring, legal structuring, and decentralized governance. The report identifies the essential elements TL inherits from TML to achieve institutional credibility: blockchain-anchored decision logs, the "No Log = No Action" mandate, and the prohibitions No Spy and No Weapon, reframed as safeguards for economic sovereignty and systemic stability. It outlines a sustainable model for an independent Ternary Logic Foundation, supported through licensing, research alliances, and transparent endowment funding. Finally, the work presents a strategic roadmap for TL's deployment across financial markets, monetary policy, and supply-chain systems, proposing phased adoption from pilot integration to standardization within critical infrastructure. By embedding verifiable memory and structured hesitation into the architecture of decision-making, Ternary Logic establishes a new evidentiary standard for resilience, transparency, and trust in economic governance.

title: Digital Platforms in the Global Food Sector

detail.title: Digital Platforms in the Global Food Sector
detail.abstract: Active use of digital platforms in the global food sector aims to increase production efficiency, optimize product distribution, improve demand profile, and address social issues in the raw materials and processing areas of the food sector. The most actively developing platforms in this sector are production, market, and educational platforms. Open digital platforms, primarily geospatial, information and knowledge ones, have proven their effectiveness. The positive effects of using digital platforms in the food sector include increased labor productivity, integration of all types of resources, optimization of managerial and organizational decisions, and the negative effects include a change in the competitive environment in favor of large business entities and the distortion of the labor market.

detail.abstract: This article examines how AI's economic engine is shifting from data-fueled growth to a system driven by attribution capacity. As generative AI consumes freely available data, the ability to trace value back to human and institutional sources becomes the key determinant of long-term sustainability. Drawing on industry developments and emerging platform dynamics, the paper argues that 2026 will mark a turning point when competition centers less on model capability and more on attribution infrastructure, enabling a transition from AI-driven job displacement toward AI-enabled income distribution.

detail.abstract: Traditional financial theory assumes rational market participants, yet markets are often influenced by emotions and sentiment. Using a new and comprehensive sample dataset of 155,740 Reddit posts and comments referencing S&P 100 firms from seven major financial subreddits between 2015 and May 2025, this study explores the predictive power of social media sentiment. The research introduces novel Reddit engagement metrics to enhance sentiment quality assessment and incorporates the sentiment results using a multi-timeframe trading strategy. The empirical results show significant predictive power with compounded returns of 216,103% compared to the S&P buy-and-hold return of 225% over the sample period. Importantly, the study reveals that sentiment analysis becomes most valuable during periods of market uncertainty, such as the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2022 inflationary downturn. Understanding the sentiment of social media data has become increasingly important as individual investors continue to adopt these new forms of communication.

detail.abstract: This study proposes a new theoretical model describing the internal composition and functionality of black holes. Contrary to the classical view that considers black holes as singularities of infinite density and zero volume, this paper presents a multidimensional structure governed by dynamic equilibrium between energy absorption, transformation, and regeneration. The black hole is redefined as a multidimensional energy-matter recycling system operating through three interdependent zones: the Absorption Field, the Combustion-Reconfiguration Core, and the Expansion Displacement Field. Each zone performs a specific physical function that collectively sustains the black hole as an engine of cosmic regeneration. This framework integrates principles from the universe recycling through black holes, Omnia Mobilis (Ruiz Estrada, 2011), and the Dynamic Imbalance State (DIS) model (Ruiz Estrada, M.A. and Yap, S.F., 2013), establishing a new perspective on how energy and matter evolve, invert, and expand through multidimensional interactions within black holes.

title: Pathwise Greeks for Barrier Options under Rough Volatility: Smoothing and CRN Bumps

detail.title: Pathwise Greeks for Barrier Options under Rough Volatility: Smoothing and CRN Bumps
detail.abstract: We study Delta estimation for up-and-out barrier options under rough volatility, with rough Bergomi as the default model and a rough-Heston cross-check. We compare two strategies that are unbiased in the limit: (i) central finite-difference bumps with common random numbers (CRN) in the bump size h ↓ 0, and (ii) a smoothed-pathwise (SPW) estimator that replaces the barrier indicator by a differentiable Brownian-bridge-based proxy, consistent as the smoothing ε ↓ 0 (and ∆t ↓ 0 for continuous monitoring). Using a fast-convolution discretization of the Volterra kernel, we report RMSE-versus-time, variance, and equal-wall-clock comparisons. Across configurations, SPW achieves lower equal-budget variance and faster RMSE decay than CRN while matching CRN means within 95% confidence intervals, supporting the absence of material bias at practical (h, ε).

title: Accelerating Industrial Decarbonisation: The Role of Tax Incentives
affiliations: , , Imperial College London, , , University Paris Dauphine and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Accelerating Industrial Decarbonisation: The Role of Tax Incentives
detail.abstract: This discussion note examines how tax incentives can support industrial decarbonisation. Achieving net-zero targets in industrial sectors will require substantial investment in low-carbon technologies, especially in “hard-to-abate” industries such as steel, cement, and petrochemicals. In this context, tax incentives have emerged as a useful policy instrument, in combination with carbon pricing, regulation and further measures. Countries are already deploying a wide range of targeted tax incentives to accelerate the adoption of low-carbon electricity. Examples include investment tax credits for clean energy equipment (e.g., France) and accelerated depreciation for investments into renewables (e.g., Canada). Tax incentives are also a core pillar of decarbonisation efforts in the transport sector – including accelerated uptake of electric vehicles. Many countries support electric vehicles (EVs) with measures spanning from production tax credits (e.g., Japan) to consumer tax incentives (e.g., United States). A similar wave of incentives is emerging to advance green hydrogen and lower-carbon technologies in steel, cement and petrochemicals. Many governments are supporting businesses investing to produce green hydrogen with tax credits and corporate income tax exemptions (e.g., Egypt). Several countries have introduced incentives for lower-carbon steel production including abatement via CCUS (e.g., Malaysia). Similar incentives pertain to green cement and petrochemicals (e.g., Finland). Overall, tax incentives supporting industrial decarbonisation can open the door to a faster low-carbon transition. They can help in reaching the necessary production scale of new technologies to reduce costs. They can support the adoption of new products and services to trigger positive network effects. And they can reduce uncertainty around technological trajectories and related hurdles for investments. To that end, clear objectives, effective design and robust evaluation frameworks are critical. Tax incentives can lead to high fiscal costs. They may trigger premature technology choices. When supporting demand, such as for electric vehicles and other consumer goods, they can exacerbate inequality. Transparency on goals, clear eligibility criteria, robust monitoring and evaluation, as well as sunset clauses are essential to address these challenges. Alignment with broader industrial and decarbonisation strategies is also key. Tax incentives should not be used as stand-alone instruments, but rather as key components of broader policy packages for industrial decarbonisation. They are complements, not substitutes, for other measures, such as carbon pricing, phasing out fossil fuel subsidies, and direct investment in infrastructure When deployed in that manner, tax incentives can be a critical catalyst to accelerate industrial decarbonisation.

title: Removable Batteries as a Case Study for Right to Repair Legislation: A Markovian Stochastic Model for Determining Legislative Impact on Device Longevity
affiliations: Bergen County Academies

detail.title: Removable Batteries as a Case Study for Right to Repair Legislation: A Markovian Stochastic Model for Determining Legislative Impact on Device Longevity
detail.abstract:
This study aims to quantify the impact of right-to-repair legislation on smartphone longevity and e-waste. Recent EU regulation proposals will require manufacturers to use removable batteries in smartphones to extend device lifetimes by 2027. This paper uses a Markovian stochastic model to simulate the smartphone life cycle based on this proposal, whilst also providing a framework for future pieces of legislation. The model compares current durability trends and a scenario with mandated battery removability by introducing a new state into the Markov Chain. Even considering a conservative repair-adoption scenario, where adoption rates of repair stay constant to the status quo, the model predicts an average smartphone lifespan increase from 2.5 to 2.66 years (6.4%). In a best-case scenario of 100% adoption of battery repair, average lifespan extends to 3.08 years (23.2%).

The changes in lifespan can be analyzed from an environmental lens. Using 2030 estimates of smartphone consumption, an estimated maximum of 3,700 metric tons of e-waste and 1.75 million metric tons of CO₂-equivalent emissions per cycle of smartphone purchases would be avoided in the EU market alone. Our conservative estimates 1200 metric tons of e-waste and 559,350 tons of CO₂-equivalent emissions. The wide range demonstrates that legislation can yield measurably high sustainability gains, but benefits otherwise depend on consumer repair adoption rates. The model provides a replicable framework to isolate and quantify single design interventions, to better inform future right-to-repair legislation with a data-driven approach.

title: Influence Of Robotics Integration on Students' Attitudes, Interest, And Motivation Towards Stem Learning: A Systematic Review

detail.title: Influence Of Robotics Integration on Students' Attitudes, Interest, And Motivation Towards Stem Learning: A Systematic Review
detail.abstract: Incorporation of robotics in education is estimated to be a solution that can increase the interest and motivation of students in learning STEM. There is hardly any systematic evidence regarding how robotics influence affects affective outcomes such as attitudes, curiosity, and motivation in the context of African education. The current research rigorously discusses empirical research on the effect of robotics integration on students' attitude, interest, and motivation toward STEM education, specifically within the African learning environment. The study also aims to identify current gaps and methodological weaknesses in the existing literature. The review encompassed 50 peer-reviewed empirical articles published during the period between 2021 and 2025, selected from leading academic databases like ERIC, Scopus, ResearchGate, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and African Journals Online. The review followed the PRISMA 2020 template to ensure transparency and reproducibility. Targeted search strings and Boolean operators guided the studies' selection. A data extraction matrix was used to draw out central details like authorship, educational level, study design, type of robotics intervention, affective variables measured, and results. This indicate that robotics integration positively contributed to the attitude, interest, and motivation of students towards STEM learning. Important limitations were reported, including the prevalence of short-term interventions, absence of standardized measures, and few African-based studies. The study concludes that robotics education has strong potential to increase affective interest in STEM learning in African environments. Future studies, however, must target theory-based, longitudinal designs taking into consideration contextual factors such as teacher training, equity, and access to technology. The findings have important implications for policymakers, curriculum designers, and educators for advocating robotics-based STEM education in Africa.

title: Option Pricing as a Dynamic Nash Equilibrium: A Game-Theoretic Derivation of the Black-Scholes Model
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Option Pricing as a Dynamic Nash Equilibrium: A Game-Theoretic Derivation of the Black-Scholes Model
detail.abstract: We rederive the Black-Scholes option pricing equation as the dynamic Nash equilibrium of a repeated zero-sum game between a hedger and Nature. In discrete time, the hedger's mixed strategy-a probabilistic mixture between buying, selling, and holding the underlying assetand Nature's mixed strategy-a probabilistic mixture of up/down moves-jointly determine the unique equilibrium price equal to the discounted expectation under the risk-neutral measure. In continuous time, the same principle yields a differential game between the hedger and an adversarial market drift; its Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation collapses to the Black-Scholes partial differential equation. This game-theoretic formulation provides a natural unification of replication, risk-neutral pricing, and Nash equilibrium.

detail.title: The Economics of Insurance Guaranty Funds
detail.abstract: Growing climate risk is straining P&C insurers' financial stability. State-level guaranty funds are designed to protect consumers facing insolvent insurers, yet their structure and effectiveness remain understudied. Unlike the pre-funded and centralized FDIC, these guaranty funds are state-run and rely on ex-post, risk-insensitive assessments of surviving insurers. While guaranty funds are intended to increase trust in the insurance system, in practice payouts can take years to reach homeowners, leaving them with unrepaired homes as they wait for claims to be paid. Crucially, we find that their structure significantly distorts insurance supply: solvent insurers exit states following insolvencies to avoid these "tax" assessments and to escape inheriting concentrated exposures in affected counties. Furthermore, the post-funding mechanism degrades supply quality: fragile insurers, ignoring their own insolvency costs, underprice better-capitalized rivals for fully covered policies. Other explanations of exit, such as general industry-wide declines or climate risk management do not explain these exit and pricing patterns, though they can amplify the effects of the guaranty fund. These findings highlight how the current guaranty fund design induces moral hazard and amplifies pro-cyclical supply disruptions.

detail.title: Credit Card Company and Liquidity Provision
detail.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how a credit card company can effectively assist investors in hedging against liquidity risk. By leveraging the institutional features of credit cards, we demonstrate that this mechanism outperforms traditional demandable deposits by addressing the panic-driven bank-run problem identified by Diamond and Dybvig (1983) and by being resilient to the potential trading opportunities discussed by Jacklin (1987). More broadly, we provide a strategic rationale for why narrow banking can contribute to stabilizing our economy.

detail.title: The Lottery of Luck: Why Education Remains the Only Scalable Path to Middle-Class Stability in the AI Economy
detail.abstract: The importance of higher education in the age of AI. It asserts that higher education remains the most scalable way for individuals to achieve and maintain middleclass status, citing OECD data showing that adults with a bachelor’s degree earn about 39% more than those with only a secondary education, with even greater benefits for advanced degrees. In the U.S., the poverty rate among those with a bachelor’s degree or higher is roughly three times lower than among high school diploma holders. While recognizing success stories of those without degrees, the passage highlights that platform economies like Twitter and YouTube demonstrate extreme income concentration at the top, making outlier success paths difficult for most to replicate. It emphasizes that AI amplifies existing human capital—serving as a GPS rather than a driver—and stresses the importance of treating education as essential economic infrastructure. The proposed reforms include universal foundational skills, integrating AI and data literacy into education, and promoting lifelong re-skilling through tax and employment policies. Ultimately, education is presented as the key tool to turn luck into sustainable mobility. Across the OECD, bachelor’s-level attainment is associated with roughly 40% higher earnings than upper-secondary, and significantly lower poverty and unemployment risks; in U.S. data, the gaps between BA and HS are around 66% in median weekly earnings, about 1.7 percentage points in unemployment, and roughly nine percentage points in poverty for adults aged 25 and over, consistent with education being the only scalable path to middle-class stability.

detail.abstract: The essay, "The Inevitability of Artificial Intelligence: A Philosophical Inquiry into Morality, Ethics, and Finance," explores the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) as an unavoidable stage in the evolution of human cognition and economic organization. Through a synthesis of moral philosophy, technological ethics, and financial theory, the paper argues that AI's integration into finance is not merely a technological progression but a metaphysical inevitability reflecting humanity's drive to externalize its own intelligence. It examines the ethical tension between algorithmic optimization and moral reasoning, emphasizing that machines, while capable of simulating rational choice, cannot possess moral intent. The discussion situates this dilemma within the financial sector, highlighting issues of accountability, fairness, and transparency in algorithmic decision-making. The paper concludes that while AI cannot be halted, it can be guided by ethical stewardship-where human judgment remains the moral compass of technological progress. Ultimately, the inevitability of AI represents not the diminishment of humanity but the reawakening of its ethical responsibility in an increasingly automated world.

title: Risk-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Crypto and Equity Trading Under Transaction Costs

detail.title: Risk-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Crypto and Equity Trading Under Transaction Costs
detail.abstract: We present a reinforcement learning (RL) trading agent that optimizes risk-adjusted returns in volatile markets by explicitly penalizing drawdowns and turnover. Our approach uses Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to learn long/flat/short positioning in Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), and SPY. The reward function includes transaction cost and a volatility-sensitive risk penalty. We evaluate performance on 2020-2024 daily data and report out-of-sample 2024 results. The learned RL policy achieved a Sharpe ratio of 1.23 versus 1.46 for a buy-and-hold benchmark, with a final NAV of 1.916 compared to 2.213. Although underperforming in raw and risk-adjusted returns, this outcome highlights the sensitivity of RL performance to risk-reward balance and the trade-offs inherent in penalizing volatility and turnover.

detail.title: Determinants of narrative risk disclosure in the insurance sector: evidence from German Solvency and Financial Condition Reports

publicationDetails.detailsText: In: The Journal of Risk Finance, https://doi.org/10.1108/JRF-04-2024-0106 (online first 03. November 2025)

detail.abstract:
Purpose

This study aims to provide initial evidence on the determinants of insurers’ narrative risk disclosure in Solvency and Financial Condition Reports (SFCRs) as a new reporting instrument under Solvency II.

Design/methodology/approach

We investigate the volume of risk disclosure collected from 1,510 solo SFCRs by 302 unique German (non-listed and listed) insurers over the reporting periods 2016–2020. Based on socio-political theories, we hypothesise that risk disclosure volume is positively associated with insurer size and status as a life insurer and negatively associated with the insurer’s solvency ratio and legal form as an insurer governed by public law.

Findings

Our results support our hypotheses and suggest that socio-political theories explain the variations in risk disclosure volume in SFCRs. The key results remain unaltered when focusing on the disclosure of insurers’ risk profiles and hold for various robustness tests. Additionally, our study provides novel insights into how narrative risk disclosure relates to disclosure regulations and insurers’ institutional characteristics.

Social implications

Our findings imply that public (social and political) pressure on insurers drives their narrative risk disclosure to the broad public.

Originality/value

To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to explore the determinants of risk disclosure in SFCRs. By doing so, it enriches the limited research on risk disclosure in the insurance sector and overcomes the shortcomings of prior studies that focus on grouplevel evidence from the financial reports of listed insurers.

detail.abstract: This resolution extends three decades of externally managed interventions whose outcomes have been ambiguous or damaging. On 30 September 2025, the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 2793, authorizing a new ―Gang Suppression Force‖ (GSF) to replace the Kenya-led Multinational Security Support Mission (MSS) in Haiti. The mission carries a 12-month mandate, a projected strength of 5,500 personnel, and logistical backing from a newly established UN Support Office in Haiti (UNSOH). While framed as an urgent measure to restore security, this resolution perpetuates a model of dependency that undermines Haitian sovereignty. This article examines Resolution 2793 through historical, political, and policy lenses. It argues that the GSF perpetuates structural dependency and sidesteps lessons from previous missions, including failures of accountability, sovereignty erosion, and public-health harm such as the 2010 cholera outbreak. Drawing on documentary analysis, policy reports, and comparative peacekeeping literature, the study evaluates the GSF’s likely efficacy and legitimacy. It concludes by proposing a Haitian-centered policy model for national security architecture grounded in sovereignty, accountability, and national ownership.

detail.abstract: Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) models are very popular for analyzing a wide range of policy issues. CGE applications vary from estimating the welfare impact of tax reform and alternative energy policies to the effect of foreign trade reforms, labour markets and employment. CGE models are commonly developed at the country level; however, modified versions of CGE, so called Regional CGE (RCGE) models, can be used at subnational disaggregation to examine impacts studied at the national counterparts on a specific region. RCGE models have grown in popularity as an alternative to the Input-Output (I-O) models, which are regularly used for regional analysis. RCGE models can provide comprehensive information, which make them more desirable analytical models for many researchers. Yet, RCGE models have not yet become a "go-to" for governmental policy practitioners when they are developing regional public policies. This paper reviews the current state of regional CGE models, describes their features, contributions and limitations and surveys some applications of the main three classes of RCGE models: region-specific, bottom-up, and top-down models. This paper concludes that the applications of RCGE are quite variable and flexible, with a new and more complex type of application to be developed with the advancement of computation economics. The paper offers recommendations on the micro, meso and macro conditions that are necessary to increase policy practitioners' utilization of RCGE models.

title: The onshoring of private purpose trusts in Scotland
affiliations: School of Law, University of Edinburgh

detail.title: The onshoring of private purpose trusts in Scotland
detail.abstract:
Over the course of the past 30 or so years, offshore jurisdictions have pushed the boundaries of trust law, often with the objective of attracting and competing for foreign investment. Some of these offshore innovations have reached onshore territories. This is not entirely surprising, for it is not uncommon for legislatures to draw on foreign models and, at times, to transplant foreign instruments into their own home jurisdiction. However, in the context of trust law, legal scholars have expressed concerns about such developments, especially because offshore jurisdictions have developed types of trusts that have taken the trust concept to its limits and that can be put to all manner of uses. 

This article provides a comprehensive examination of an example of such onshoring of a foreign type of trust in Scotland: the introduction of private purpose trusts in the Trusts and Succession (Scotland) Act 2024. It shows that the drafters of this new Act (which for the most part is not yet in force) have heavily drawn on offshore models whilst also going a step further in providing a legal framework for private purpose trusts that is even more flexible and settlor-friendly than some of the offshore instruments that have inspired it. This framework raises several concerns related especially to the (i) lack of accountability of trustees and supervisors of Scottish private purpose trusts; (ii) the enforceability of such trusts more generally; (iii) the permissive and open textured nature of some of the legislative provisions; as well as (iv) their scope and impact on the rights of potential beneficiaries under such trusts. More fundamentally, there is a danger that these private purpose trusts will be used to create a vacuum in beneficial entitlement to property. While many of these concerns are not unique to Scotland, as the article shows, they are heightened by some of the choices that the Scottish drafters have made and certain specific features of Scottish trust law within which the new framework will operate. The article further illustrates that despite the ambitions of the drafters, the new framework may not necessarily attract greater international investments in Scotland nor lead to more trust business for the Scottish legal profession. It also argues that its effects are not necessarily limited to Scotland.

detail.abstract: Many Americans with serious mental illness lack access to inpatient psychiatric care. For decades, Medicaid's "institutions for mental diseases" (IMD) exclusion has been a major barrier to expanding psychiatric hospital bed capacity, but the ongoing mental-health crisis has recently led some policymakers to consider repealing or modifying the IMD exclusion. detail.title: Multi-Asset Baskets under Rough Volatility: Low-Rank Features and Importance Sampling for Control Variates
detail.abstract: We study Monte Carlo pricing of European basket options under rough volatility in moderate to high dimension. We build learned, centered control variates (CVs) from low-rank features of multi-asset paths (terminal log-returns, per-asset min/max, realized variance) reduced by PCA or random projections; we combine this with a simple market-mode importance sampling (IS) tilt with a closed-form likelihood ratio (LR). A small independent pilot fits both the low-rank predictor and the IS tilt; the pricing batch reuses them, preserving unbiasedness and preventing overfit. On synthetic rough-Bergomi baskets up to d = 20, the method delivers substantial empirical variance reduction (EVR), increasing with dimension and stabilizing with modest ranks.

detail.title: HyperDetect-Football: Bidirectional Detail Propagation and Hypergraph Context Aggregation for Robust Football Detection in Long-Range Images
detail.abstract: In long-shot football videos, critical objects such as the ball are often extremelysmall (typically smaller than 10×10 pixels) and suffer from challenges includinghigh-speed motion, occlusion, and complex background clutter, making themdifficult to detect reliably. Current mainstream lightweight detectors—such asYOLOv5n and YOLOv8n—still struggle with insufficient spatial detail preservation and inadequate contextual modeling. To address these limitations, wepropose HyperDetect-Football, a hypergraph-enhanced small object detectionmethod. Our approach introduces, for the first time in a lightweight framework,a high-resolution P2 detection branch with stride=4 to significantly enhance spatial awareness of tiny objects. We further design a HyperCompute Module thatexplicitly captures high-order semantic dependencies across scales and spatiallocations via learnable hyperedges. Additionally, a bidirectional feature fusionmechanism is developed to enable closed-loop interaction between low-level details and high-level semantics. Experiments on the SoccerNet_v3_H250 datasetshow that HyperDetect-Football achieves a mAP@0.5 of 75.0% and an AP@0.5of 53.2% for the ball class, substantially outperforming YOLOv5n (39.7%) andYOLOv8n (38.5%) by +13.5 and +14.7 percentage points, respectively, whileusing only 1.84M parameters— 39% fewer than YOLOv8n. Qualitative results further demonstrate the robustness and practicality of our method under challenging conditions such as motion blur, color confusion, and severe occlusion.

detail.abstract: The COM-B model, widely adopted in behaviour change research, systematically explores and categorises the behav- ioural barriers and facilitators to inform intervention design. The model highlights that where the right mix of barriers and facilitators, in the broad categories of capability, motivation, and opportunity exist, a given behaviour is more likely to be enacted. However, for wicked problems, applying the COM-B model becomes challenging due to complexity, uncertainty, manageability challenges, and the interpretative opacity of the systems that influence behaviour. This paper introduces a combined framework (SeCOM-B) that integrates the Socio-ecological model (SEM) and the COM-B model, highlighting its potential application in co-designing behaviour change interventions to address wicked problems, which often involve non-scientific stakeholders and interdisciplinary team members. Drawing on three case studies of practical behaviour change projects taking place in Australia (2) and Vietnam (1) between March 2022 and July 2023, the paper further illustrates the application of the SeCOM-B model in analysing the drivers and barriers of behaviours, and explor- ing the implications for intervention design.

publicationDetails.journalName: Canadian Tax Foundation (CTF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The Income Tax Act and the Excise Tax Act impose penalties on taxpayers who fail to comply with their obligations “knowingly” or “under circumstances amounting to gross negligence” (“KGN penalties”). The case law has established a high threshold for “gross negligence,” holding that it requires the taxpayer to have shown “a high degree of negligence tantamount to intentional acting.” The minister of national revenue bears the onus to prove the facts supporting the imposition of a KGN penalty.

Since 2018, in appeals of KGN penalties that proceed to judgment, the Tax Court of Canada has completely vacated the penalties approximately 30 percent of the time, on the basis that either there was no non-compliance by the taxpayer, or the taxpayer’s non-compliance was unintentional and did not result from a high degree of negligence tantamount to intentional acting.

In the civil courts, as endorsed by the Supreme Court of Canada, adverse cost consequences can result when a party alleges fraud or dishonest conduct and fails to prove the allegations (“the fraud costs rule”). This article argues that the Tax Court should adopt the fraud costs rule and allow taxpayers to claim enhanced costs when the Crown fails to meet its burden of proof when litigating a KGN penalty. Allowing taxpayers to presumptively claim such costs would, it is hoped, motivate the minister to take greater care when deciding whether to assess and litigate KGN penalties, which
would in turn help to avoid the unfortunate situation—of which many troubling examples exist—of KGN penalties being unreasonably and improperly proposed or imposed on taxpayers.

title: Can the UK meet the World Health Organization PM2.5 interim target of 10 μg m-3 by 2030? Part II: Associated Health and Economic Benefits

detail.title: Can the UK meet the World Health Organization PM2.5 interim target of 10 μg m-3 by 2030? Part II: Associated Health and Economic Benefits
detail.abstract: Air pollution has extensive, adverse impacts on human health throughout the life course. This study estimated the health and economic benefits that policy at country and city level can have on the UK achieving the PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter <2.5 μm) WHO interim target of 10 μg m-3. Here we quantify and monetise the health benefits using lifetable analysis from the air pollution concentrations created using sophisticated chemical transport models. Modelling predictions in 2030 were made by combining European Union and UK government’s emissions forecasts, with the Climate Change Committee’s Net Zero (NZ) Electric vehicle (EV) forecasts, and in London with the addition of local policies. UK health and monetary benefits of air pollution reductions up to 2030 were substantial with the UK population gaining 11.5 (8.7–12.8) million life years, equivalent to an improvement in average life expectancy of 2 months and monetised air pollution benefits of £218 to £300 billion (summed to 2134). The conclusions from this study contributes to the evidence base on health benefits to advocate for action and are therefore highly relevant to policy makers. From an economic perspective, this study shows that air-pollution-reduction policies costing up to £2.4 (1.8–2.7) billion per year would be justified. Furthermore, the issues addressed here, such as the co-benefit of NZ policy on EV combined with international, national and local policies toward meeting WHO targets, offer a global public health opportunity of major significance for this century and could be applicable to other international cities.

detail.title: The Strategic Fusion of SIEM and SOAR in Modern SOCs
detail.abstract: The increasing volume and complexity of cyber threats are challenging Security Operations Centers (SOCs) to monitor, evaluate, and respond to threats in real time. This study explores the integration of Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) and Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) technologies focused on improving the efficiency of SOCs and the resilience of SOAR. By performing a literature review, comparative analysis of architectural models, and evaluation of industry-specific case studies, the research clarifies how the integration of SIEM and SOAR delivers automated data correlation, contextually aware threat prioritization, and automated workflows throughout the incident response processes. The research reveals that organizations' managed SIEM-SOAR integrations achieve the most significant positive shifts in mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR), as well as increased depth of analysis that exceeds the thresholds of machine learning with advanced threat intelligence. Furthermore, the research explores the implications of operational automation suggesting ethically bounded autonomy, defining thresholds of human involvement and machine-led processes to make optimal decisions. This study asserts that SOC modernization hinges on SIEM-SOAR integration and paves the way toward SOCs with automated security frameworks that incorporate adaptive AI for learning and positive cybersecurity posture shifting. There are implications of a paradigm change with intelligent automation to improve a cybersecurity posture while addressing the human-machine collaboration complexities for current threats.

detail.abstract: This paper develops an analytic framework for orthogonal drift elimination within the helical representation of the Zeta structure. By coupling Gaussian stationary-phase analysis with an orthogonal Mellin transport, cumulative phase drift is transformed into a single, reversible projection error. The resulting discrete-time dynamics constitute a contraction on the drift subspace, yielding exponential precision growth: the effective RMSE decreases to roughly 30% of the naive baseline and information density increases by an order of magnitude. A quantitative stabilization threshold, e λ(A)τ ρ < 1, separates controllable from entropically unstable regimes and unifies analytic, numerical, and statistical results. The mechanism reproduces, within a deterministic setting, the attenuation pattern of WKB tunneling-an entropic tunneling analogy in which orthogonality replaces dissipation. Numerical simulations confirm exponential drift suppression and phase-symmetry restoration at the stationary-phase anchors of the Riemann-Siegel lattice. This establishes a general analytic mechanism for deterministic stabilization of probabilistic systems, transforming stochastic drift into orthogonal symmetry and achieving exponential precision gain within DTIME = Θ(W (n) log(1/ε)).

detail.abstract: Climate change increases physical risks-damages from floods, storms, wildfires, droughts, heatwaves, and sea level rise. These globally accelerating risks pose a fundamental threat to economies and societies. Conventional economic analysis of climate change focuses on damages and costs/benefits of climate actions (mitigation and adaptation), relying on models that assume perfect rationality, homogeneity, and a unique equilibrium. Yet this approach falls short of capturing the complexity of physical climate risks, their inherent uncertainty, feedbacks, and adaptation responses by boundedly rational actors. Complexity economics recognizes the economy as a dynamic, adaptive system in which aggregate dynamics emerge from interactions of many boundedly rational agents who learn and update their expectations about climate and the economic consequences of their actions. This chapter discusses why embracing complexity matters for the assessment of physical climate risks and climate change adaptation strategies. Using illustrative examples from agent-based computational economics, we show how relaxing 2 traditional economic assumptions enables us to study distributional impacts and the emergence of structural shifts in markets as agents learn and interact. We highlight the importance of tracing out-of-equilibrium dynamics triggered by climate damages and adaptation responses, focusing on potential nonlinearities, including socioeconomic tipping points and potential systemic risks posed by the changing climate.

detail.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into the legal field is reshaping how legal professionals interpret, process, and utilize judicial texts. This study investigates the application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and machine learning techniques to analyze court rulings and legal opinions, aiming to uncover hidden linguistic patterns, sentiment trends, and inconsistencies in judicial reasoning. By leveraging AI-driven text analysis, the research explores how automated tools can enhance legal research, support predictive modeling of case outcomes, and contribute to a more transparent and efficient legal system. The study focuses on large-scale legal corpora from common law jurisdictions and employs a combination of pattern recognition, sentiment detection, and classification models. The findings highlight the potential of AI to not only assist legal practitioners but also transform the broader landscape of legal scholarship and policymaking. This research offers practical insights into how technology can augment traditional methods of legal analysis, raising important considerations around ethics, bias, and the future role of AI in the justice system.

title: Barrier Options under Rough Volatility: Importance Sampling + Learned Control Variates

detail.title: Barrier Options under Rough Volatility: Importance Sampling + Learned Control Variates
detail.abstract: We study variance reduction for up-and-out barrier options under rough volatility, with rough Bergomi as the default model and a rough-Heston cross-check. Our estimator combines a simple importance sampling (IS) tilt in the dominant price-Brownian direction (market mode) with a learned, centered control variate (CV) built from low-rank features of simulated paths (terminal log-returns, path extrema, realized variance) reduced via PCA or random projections. The IS tilt admits a closed-form likelihood ratio, and centering on an independent pilot preserves unbiasedness (LR-weighted under IS). Barriers are monitored on the simulation grid (discrete monitoring); continuous-monitor implications are examined via time-step refinement. Against strong baselines (plain MC, antithetic, conditional-expectation/bridge controls, quasi-MC, polynomial regression CVs), IS+CV delivers substantial empirical variance reduction and faster RMSE decay under equal wall-clock budgets, with means matching baselines within 95% confidence intervals-indicating no material bias at practical settings.

title: Price Transparency in Online Markets

detail.title: Price Transparency in Online Markets
detail.abstract: Advancements in digital technology have increased price transparency, but quality transparency has not improved significantly. As a result, more consumers (termed "shoppers") learn and compare prices of sellers, but they still need to visit each seller's website to observe its quality. We model this rise in shoppers as an increase in price transparency and examine its welfare implications in a setting where sellers compete on both price and quality. Greater price transparency reduces prices but also leads to lower and inefficient quality. It always improves consumer surplus, but can reduce total welfare if the associated efficiency loss is significant, which happens when sellers can improve quality easily but still choose low quality due to excessive price competition. Finally, we study how improving quality transparency affects welfare given the fraction of shoppers. If shoppers can also learn and compare quality, sellers will always choose the efficient level of quality. However, consumer surplus and total welfare do not necessarily increase unless quality transparency is accompanied by a certain price floor.

detail.abstract: This policy analysis addresses a critical contradiction in Ontario's long-term care reform. Despite legislative promises to enhance residents' quality of life through the Fixing Long-Term Care Act, 2021 (FLTCA), enforcement-driven regulatory mechanisms continue to perpetuate institutional models of care that undermine residents' fundamental rights to autonomy, dignity, and choice. The theoretical concern centers on the disconnect between person-centered care principles embedded in legislation and the practical implementation of punitive oversight systems that prioritize operational compliance over individualized, relational care.This concern is situated within the broader literature on healthcare policy implementation, person-centered care theory, and long-term care reform. Following decades of documented failures in institutional care models, scholars have increasingly advocated for culture change approaches that prioritize residents' autonomy and homelike environments. However, policy implementation research reveals persistent gaps between legislative intent and practice, particularly in complex healthcare systems. The COVID-19 pandemic intensified these concerns, with over 81% of Canada's COVID-related deaths occurring in long-term care homes, exposing fundamental systemic deficiencies that transcend regulatory oversight. Recent policy analysis literature emphasizes the need for transformative rather than incremental approaches to long-term care reform. This study employs a critical interpretive policy analysis approach, grounded in person-centered care principles, to examine the FLTCA 2021 and its subsequent amendment, Bill 7. Document analysis was conducted on primary legislative texts, policy documents, and related regulatory materials. The analytical framework examined contradictions between stated policy objectives and implementation mechanisms, with particular attention to how enforcement strategies align with or undermine residents' rights. The analysis considered both the explicit content of legislation, and the implicit assumptions embedded within regulatory approaches, using person-centered care theory as the evaluative lens. The analysis reveals three primary arguments supported by legislative evidence and policy outcomes. First, while the FLTCA positions long-term care homes as residents' personal homes emphasizing dignity and autonomy, the Act's enforcement mechanisms remain rooted in institutional oversight models that prioritize compliance over personalized care. Second, Bill 7's provision for non-consensual transfers directly contradicts the Residents' Bill of Rights, particularly Section 3 guaranteeing full participation in care decisions. This amendment facilitates forced admissions without informed consent, undermining core principles of autonomy and choice. Third, current policy frameworks create systemic barriers to innovative care models, particularly small home models that empirically demonstrate superior outcomes in resident satisfaction, autonomy, and quality of life. The evidence shows that despite legislative rhetoric promoting person-centered approaches, Ontario's regulatory system continues to reinforce outdated institutional paradigms that have repeatedly failed to protect residents' fundamental rights. The analysis concludes that genuine long-term care reform requires a fundamental paradigm shift from punitive oversight toward transformative, relationship-based care models. Small home models emerge as a viable alternative that operationalizes the FLTCA's stated principles while addressing residents expressed preferences for homelike environments. For international audiences, this case study demonstrates how well-intentioned healthcare legislation can inadvertently perpetuate systemic dysfunction when implementation mechanisms conflict with stated objectives. German Abstract: Angesichts einer Geburtenrate von 1,35 und eines jährlichen Defizits von 376.000 Geburten untersucht diese Studie die fiskalische Machbarkeit einer direkten Investition („Willkommensprämie“) von 50.000 € pro Neugeborenem. Unter Einbeziehung von Multiplikator-Effekten (Keynesianisch 1,37) und der langfristigen Entlastung der Sozialsysteme (GRV/GKV) wird eine positive Gesamtwirtschaftliche Bilanz nachgewiesen. English Abstract: Germany faces a severe demographic crisis with a fertility rate of 1.35, resulting in an annual deficit of 376,000 births. This Total Impact Analysis (TIA) investigates a radical fiscal intervention: a €50,000 „Welcome Bonus“ per newborn to restore the replacement rate of 2.1. Contrary to superficial cost estimates, this lifecycle analysis demonstrates a positive fiscal Net Present Value (NPV) of +€17,644 per citizen, implying a Return on Investment (ROI) of 1.10x for the state. 

The study quantifies multiplier effects (Keynesian multiplier 1.37), immediate VAT reflux (13.3% selffinancing), and massive long-term relief for social security systems (€51 billion annually after 2045). Beyond fiscal metrics, the paper evaluates strategic benefits for national defense (recruitment pool) and innovation. Addressing behavioral economic risks (deadweight loss), a progressive hybrid model is recommended. The analysis concludes that the intervention is not an expenditure but a high-yield investment, essential for safeguarding Germany’s economic and strategic future.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of financial development as a buffer for the appreciating effects of remittances on exchange rates using annual data from 1996 to 2021 for 146 economies, with a focus on 43 high remittance-receiving economies. Examining subcomponents of financial development, we find that stronger domestic financial markets and market-based financial deepening are critical channels for absorbing the REER appreciation effects of remittances.

detail.title: From Discrete Choice to Possibility- A New Method for Modelling Fuzzy and Random Uncertainties in Travel Behaviour
detail.abstract: This study introduces a novel approach for mode choice modelling based on possibility calculus theory, which addresses both randomness and fuzziness. The Max P-S technique, a fuzzy estimation process, is used to estimate the parameters within the logit model. By comparing the Max P-S technique directly with the conventional logit that uses the maximum likelihood estimation, the impact of the different estimation process is highlighted. The comparative analysis reveals that the Max P-S model consistently and significantly outperforms the MLE-based Logit model across multiple performance metrics. It achieved a substantial increase in predictive accuracy, with up to a 10% improvement on local SIDS models and a 13% increase on a Swiss model. This predictive superiority is substantiated by significantly lower RMSE and MAE values, indicating a more precise alignment with observed choices. Additionally, a lower AIC confirms the Max P-S model's superior efficiency and parsimony. Beyond prediction, the Max P-S technique provides more robust and theoretically sound explanatory power. Wald statistics demonstrated that the Max P-S technique consistently produced highly significant coefficients that align with established theory, unlike the MLE-based Logit model, which occasionally yielded problematic results. Sensitivity analysis further highlights this strength, showcasing the Max P-S technique's ability to capture realistic, non-linear behavioural thresholds and nuanced responses that are often missed by conventional Logit models. These findings underscore the value of flexible frameworks like the Max P-S technique for effective policy design and data analysis in SIDS. Future research can explore applying the Max P-S to other choice modelling techniques.

detail.title: Climate Shift Uncertainty and Economic Damages

detail.abstract: Focusing on global annual averages of climatic variables can bias aggregate and distributional estimates of the economic impacts of climate change. We here empirically identify dose-response functions of GDP growth rates to daily mean temperature levels and combine them with regional intra-annual climate projections of daily mean temperatures. We then disentangle, for various shared socio-economic pathways (SSPs), how much of the missing impacts are due to heterogeneous warming patterns over space. Global damages in 2050 are 25% (21-28% across SSPs) higher when accounting for the shift in the shape of the entire intra-annual distribution of daily mean temperatures at the regional scale.

detail.abstract: Using a large German firm survey, I randomize information on documented AI productivity gains and industry adoption rates and track firms over time. Beliefs about AI’s productivity potential rise significantly after the treatments across the prior distribution without reducing uncertainty. These treatment-induced belief shifts map into behavior: in firms where the respondent has high decision authority, AI adoption is more likely one year later. Information about competitor adoption has direct effects on actions: incumbent adopters cut prices, while not-yet adopters revise business expectations upward. Together, the results highlight the role of expectations, strategic considerations, and informational frictions in shaping technology diffusion and its macroeconomic impact.

title: Intelligent Companywide ML Optimizer for Manufactured Products: iCOMP

detail.title: Intelligent Companywide ML Optimizer for Manufactured Products: iCOMP

keywords: Digital Twin and Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming

detail.abstract: Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) companies operate in highly competitive markets characterized by rapidly changing consumer preferences, complex supply chains, and narrow profit margins. Success in this environment requires tight integration and high-performance operation between business strategies, product discovery, manufacturing operations, and consumer insights. Traditionally, these functions have operated in silos, with limited information sharing and coordination, leading to suboptimal outcomes. FMCG manufacturing is a massive real-time optimization problem that can be transformed by two technologies: a) AI machine learning analytics (ML), and b) federated computing and data infrastructures (Fenoglio and Treleaven, 2025). We envision a future where FMCG companies operate as unified, AI-driven organisms-where consumer insights flow seamlessly into product discovery, manufacturing adapts in real-time and goto-market strategies optimize continuously. This paper introduces iCOMP (Intelligent Companywide ML Optimizer for Manufactured Products) integrating a 'data-driven' companywide ML optimization approach founded upon the manufacturing domain, specifically by treating Manufacturing as the central, complex, constraint-driven optimization problem. The FMCG services are designed to support manufacturing optimization, but also include feasible inputs (Product Discovery) and maximizing the utilization and profit of its output (Go-to-Market). Five critical services constitute iCOMP: • Real-time adaptive RL action spaces: expanding or contracting based on detected consumer and competitive micro-trends. • Bi-directional feedback loop between Product Discovery and Manufacturing: via Digital Twin feasibility constraints. • Neurosymbolic Go-To-Market system: that combines symbolic reasoning for logical strategy generation with neural network pattern learning for outcome prediction, enabling adaptive market strategy optimization. • Dual-Metric Framework for Compound Optimization: Recognizing that market opportunities decay with time, iCOMP simultaneously optimizes for both speed and strategic quality by measuring Time-to-Market (TtM)-the duration to develop a feasible, highquality product using the Product Discovery and Manufacturing services-and Signal-to-Shelf (StS)-a time-normalized metric that quantifies the market impact per unit of time, driven by the Automated Trends and Go-to-Market services. This dual approach ensures rapid deployment (TtM) connected to high-quality strategic response (StS). These innovations are discussed in this paper. To illustrate iCOMP, we use development of ChillZen Coffee, a functional cold-brew beverage, which provides the framework's end-to-end operation, from consumer trend detection through product discovery, manufacturing optimization, and Go-To-Market Strategy and Actions.

detail.abstract: We provide a novel pro-competitive rationale for resale price maintenance (RPM). We consider a model where some consumers are fully informed about downstream prices while other consumers are not. When an upstream manufacturer imposes a floor on downstream prices, this qualitatively changes downstream competition---influencing not just the level, but also the dispersion, of prices. The manufacturer optimally imposes a price floor which just eliminates all downstream price dispersion, and this leads to both higher (aggregate) consumer surplus and higher total welfare as compared to the case without RPM.

detail.abstract: Property transaction prices are widely regarded as the best measure of property value, but are sometimes unavailable. Using data from the Netherlands and New York, we analyze whether list prices and assessed values are reliable substitutes. In the cross-section, both proxies strongly predict sales prices, and estimated hedonic implicit prices resemble those based on sales prices. Over time, there is a sluggish adjustment in both proxies, but much more so in assessed values - particularly when they are based on rental incomes. While assessed values are well-suited for cross-sectional hedonic modelling or the quantification of static quantitative spatial models, list prices are better suited for the estimation of hedonic implicit prices from variation over time, although some attenuation bias should be expected.
