detail.title: Exam Schools in School Choice Mechanisms: Preferences for Peer Quality versus Value-Added in New York City
detail.abstract: Exam schools are highly selective and popular among families, yet the reasons for their popularity are unclear. I study the relationships among applicant preferences, peer qualities, and school effectiveness on academic outcomes in New York City (NYC) public high schools. I jointly estimate applicant preferences for NYC exam and nonexam high schools using a unique feature of the assignment system and link those preferences to school effectiveness measures estimated using value-added regressions. I find that the higher valuation of applicants for exam schools is primarily driven by better peer quality, not by higher value-added.

title: A Real Economy Approach to Integrated Investing and Portfolio Management
affiliations: Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University and Nyenrode Business University

detail.title: A Real Economy Approach to Integrated Investing and Portfolio Management
detail.abstract:
How to invest for great financial and societal outcomes? Universal asset owners, like pension funds, play an allocational role in the real economy. At the same time, their long-run performance depends on a flourishing economy, underpinned by a thriving, livable world. Recognizing this two-way economic dependence, this chapter develops a two-step approach for asset allocation in an integrated portfolio.

In the first step, a company’s social and environmental impact is measured to determine its capacity to be future-proof. In the second step, an integrated portfolio is built with positive-impact companies and negative-impact companies that can and want to improve. The real economy approach enables universal asset owners to accelerate the transition reducing social and environmental system risks.

title: The AI Matrix as Diagnostic: Access, Agency, and Adoption

detail.title: The AI Matrix as Diagnostic: Access, Agency, and Adoption
detail.abstract: This paper operationalizes the AI Matrix (Simpson, 2025), a two axis diagnostic of Access and Agency, using public summary data to support national AI strategy. Using public data from the IMD World Digital Competitiveness Report (WDCR) 2025 subfactor ranks (N = 69 economies), we construct Access (regulatory framework, capital, technological framework) and Agency (talent, training and education, scientific concentration) by inverting ranks so 'higher means better' when graphed. Adoption is proxied by IT integration. We place countries on the AI Matrix using median splits and test the Matrix's central claim that adoption rises with both axes but is capped by the weaker side. A falsification step searches for counterexamples (top quartile adoption with one axis below its median) and finds none. Correlations computed on inverted composites (Pearson) and as a rank based check (Spearman) show the strongest association between Adoption and the bottleneck proxy minimum (Access, Agency), not with an average or a difference. Robustness is probed by swapping the adoption proxy (cloud or ERP series), checking short run movement across adjacent years, and adding a light equity overlay (usage, trust, affordability) to guard against national average bias. We provide a minimal replication bundle and a Transition Playbook that translates Matrix position into near term policy actions. Limitations are noted (ordinal ranks, perceptual signal, within country heterogeneity). Even so, the AI Matrix offers a transparent, reproducible orientation tool for coordinated decision-making and a bridge to further deeper causal analysis.

title: Automated ESG Prediction through Artificial Intelligence: A Literature-Driven Empirical Synthesis and Framework for Future Research
affiliations: RVITM, RVITM and RVITM

detail.title: Automated ESG Prediction through Artificial Intelligence: A Literature-Driven Empirical Synthesis and Framework for Future Research
detail.abstract: Recent advances in AI have revolutionized ESG analytics by extracting sustainability insights from unstructured financial and news text. This study reviews current methods for ESG prediction using NLP, ensemble learning, and deep time-series models. It highlights the strong performance of transformer-based and hybrid CNN-Transformer architectures, alongside challenges in data bias, rating inconsistency, and interpretability. A framework is proposed for multimodal data fusion, cross-provider calibration, and explainable model design, addressing both ethical and practical aspects of sustainable AI.

title: The Timing of Taxes: Labor Supply Responses over the Year

detail.title: The Timing of Taxes: Labor Supply Responses over the Year
detail.abstract: How does labor supply respond to a change in the timing of tax payments? I leverage a natural experiment in France that increased the frequency of income tax payments, shifting from three quarterly installments to twelve monthly deductions, holding the total tax burden constant. Using matched survey and administrative data, I apply a triple difference-in-differences strategy and estimate a decrease in hours worked by 2 percent, concentrated in months newly subject to payment. These findings are in line with predictions of an inattentive agent model in which taxes are more salient in periods in which they are paid. Following a sufficient statistic approach, I map the reform's effect into a wage-equivalent change. Due to a lack of salience, a 10 percent tax increase reduces hours only by an 8.55 percent cut in the gross wage. Since the reduction in hours comes mainly from workers shirking at work, the findings imply that inattention acts as a positive productivity externality.

title: PPT Discretionary Relief: Taxpayer's Right or Tax Power?
affiliations: Brazilian Institute of Tax Law (IBDT) and

detail.title: PPT Discretionary Relief: Taxpayer's Right or Tax Power?
detail.abstract: This article analyzes the legal nature of the so-called discretionary relief, a concept included in the 2017 OECD Commentary to Article 29 of the Model Tax Convention (para. 10), although absent from the clause's normative wording. This mechanism may allow either the granting of the same benefit that would have applied absent abuse ("relief 1"), or a different treaty benefit upon recharacterization of the transaction ("relief 2"). The paper investigates whether this relief constitutes a mere administrative faculty or a taxpayer's subjective right-and whether, if a right, it must be expressly provided in the treaty to be enforceable. The analysis is grounded in a systematic reading of the OECD Commentary and considers constitutional and international legal limits on tax authority discretion. The article also compares how different jurisdictions interpret the Principal Purpose Test (PPT) and General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAARs), especially in treaty abuse cases. It examines the boundaries of discretion, burden of proof, and legal standards such as proportionality, good faith, and procedural guarantees. Ultimately, it argues for the adoption of coherent, rights-based interpretive criteria in the post-BEPS era, promoting legal certainty and limiting arbitrariness. It identifies a trend toward international harmonization that respects both anti abuse objectives and fundamental taxpayer protections.

detail.abstract: India's electric vehicle (EV) sector has experienced rapid expansion over the past decade. However, can the current growth trajectory enable India to realistically achieve its ambitious target of 30% EV penetration by 2030? Using disaggregated registration data from the VAHAN dashboard (2001-2025) and appropriate time-series forecasting techniques, this article shows that two-wheelers and three-wheelers have gained significant momentum. However, four-wheelers, buses, and commercial vehicles, that is, the segments with the highest emissions intensity, remain at a low-adoption equilibrium. Under business-as-usual conditions, India is likely to achieve only 8-10% EV penetration by 2030. We attribute this shortfall to structural factors, including uneven charging infrastructure, regional disparities, and dependence on imported battery components. Our analysis suggests that India's firstgeneration, subsidy-driven policies are reaching their limits. A second generation of reforms, centred on public-fleet electrification, manufacturing localization, and integrated charging ecosystems, is essential for a realistic and equitable transition.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how international buyers’ market power and transport mode shape the pass-through of exchange rate shocks to export prices. Using transaction level customs data from the Bangladeshi garment sector, we first document substantial buyer market power and the concentration of export activity in key trade hubs that shape transport decisions. We then show that large buyers leverage both their market power and their reliance on air freight to mitigate the impact of exchange rate fluctuations. Taken together, our findings highlight how buyer characteristics shape exporters’ adjustment to external shocks, with broader implications for regional economic resilience.

title: The impact of AI on the European financial sector and the role of social dialogue
affiliations: Associazione per gli Studi Internazionali e Comparati sul Diritto del lavoro e sulle Relazioni industriali (ADAPT) and Associazione per gli Studi Internazionali e Comparati sul Diritto del lavoro e sulle Relazioni industriali (ADAPT)

detail.title: The impact of AI on the European financial sector and the role of social dialogue

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Developed within the framework of the EU co-funded project FinAI*, subtitled an Anthropocentric approach to AI to support people and companies. Developing social dialogue on the e-skills of workers in the European financial sector (n. 101145653), this paper aims to examine the intersection between artificial intelligence (AI) and labour relations in the financial sector, with a particular focus on the role of social dialogue and collective bargaining in fostering ethical AI adoption. 

The research adopts a mixed-method approach, integrating legal analysis and case studies. First, the paper analyses Regulation EU 2024/1689 (the AI Act), focusing on its key provisions. The national-level implementation of the Act is assessed through a comparative review of legislation in selected Member States and candidate countries, focusing on social partner involvement. 

In addition to the legal analysis, the study collects and examines social dialogue and collective bargaining best practices through a review of collective agreements, social partner declarations and sectoral/company-level initiatives. 

The research reveals a general lack of multi-stakeholder processes in the development and adoption of AI-related regulations at the European and national levels, with limited social partner engagement. However, it also identifies several examples of effective social dialogue and collective bargaining practices that promote ethical AI use. In this sense, this paper aims to highlight the critical role of social dialogue in ensuring a human-centred approach to AI in the workplace, advocating for closer involvement of social partners in the governance of AI technologies.

title: Applicability of the Poison Pill in the Nigerian Corporate System
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Applicability of the Poison Pill in the Nigerian Corporate System
detail.abstract: Back in the 80s, Corporate activities were at their peak. Mergers and acquisitions were going on everywhere, and people started introducing debt financing and bonds as tools to buy companies by force through what is called hostile takeovers. To curb this, Martin Lipton, developed a system called the poison pills to prevent these takeovers. He created a system that allowed existing shareholders to buy shares at a discount, making it expensive for the trying to takeover to succeed. It was effective. But can this same tool be used to stop takeovers in Nigeria? After examining the legal framework, the reality is that the Poison Pill doesn't fit into our legal system. Under CAMA 2020, it is basically impossible. We have rules against issuing shares at a discount, and with the removal of "Authorised Share Capital," directors can no longer keep extra shares on the shelf to use as a defence. Since the Poison Pill is off the table, does that mean Nigerian founders are helpless? No. This paper explores valid alternatives like Staggered Boards and Shareholder Agreements that offer similar protection while staying compliant with the Nigerian laws.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Legal Education: Current Practices, Debates, and Recommendations
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania,

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Legal Education: Current Practices, Debates, and Recommendations

publicationDetails.journalName: JusGov Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into legal education marks a turning point for law schools’ traditionally conservative pedagogical practices. AI tools now assist with legal research, writing, instruction, and personalized learning, offering opportunities to enhance both efficiency and pedagogical reach. Simultaneously, their use raises ethical and implementation concerns for legal educators. This paper presents a structured review of AI adoption in legal education, with a focus on both global and Portuguese contexts. Drawing on an analysis of 50 legal education AI tools that support English and/or Portuguese, this paper categorizes their functions, reviews current applications, and surveys the academic literature debating their pedagogical merits and drawbacks. While scholarship has discussed theoretical implications of AI in law schools and higher education, it often lacks a comprehensive catalogue of specific tools and their educational uses. In response, this study provides a technical mapping of available tools and concludes with recommendations for their integration into law school curricula – particularly within Portuguese legal education.

title: Productivity and Public Investment Rethinking the EU’s Debt Sustainability Analysis

detail.title: Productivity and Public Investment Rethinking the EU’s Debt Sustainability Analysis

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper identifies public investment as an efficient and significant tool for addressing the issue of the widening productivity gap between the EU and its main trading partners. Specifically, the paper estimates the impact of net public investment growth on net private investment growth and non-agricultural private sector labour productivity growth, excluding the real estate sector. Results suggest that an ambitious public investment strategy might be able to steer private investment and boost productivity growth. Additionally, the paper assesses whether the debt sustainability analysis (DSA) framework employed by the European Commission would allow the implementation of an ambitious public investment programme or impose constraints, instead. The structure of the DSA framework suffers from four fundamental flaws: (i) the estimation of potential output merely replicates national account identities; (ii) the output gap is inefficient in capturing inflationary dynamics and hysteresis effects; (iii) investment in general, and public investment in particular, is undermined in the DSA framework; and (iv) the fiscal multipliers assumed by the European Commission are unrealistically small. Given these flaws, the DSA framework ought to be re-contextualised in order to support the implementation of a public investment strategy.

title: The Right to Meaningful Explanation in Algorithmic Management: Commentary on the CJEU's judgment in Dun & Bradstreet Austria, Case C-203/22
affiliations: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI)

detail.title: The Right to Meaningful Explanation in Algorithmic Management: Commentary on the CJEU's judgment in Dun & Bradstreet Austria, Case C-203/22

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Introduction 

Automated decision-making (ADM) systems in the workplace give rise to structural information asymmetries, impinge on the protection of workers’ personal data and raise questions of accountability. These systems, which are often opaque, have significant legal and economic consequences for workers. On 27 February 2025 the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) delivered its judgment in CK v Dun & Bradstreet Austria GmbH (Case C-203/22),1 clarifying key provisions under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR):

 (1) The scope of the right of access to information under Article 15(1)(h) GDPR, which confers on data subjects the right to receive ‘meaningful information about the logic involved’ in automated decision-making.

 (2) What qualifies as ‘meaningful information about the logic involved’ in ADM systems, as set out in Article 22(3), which applies only to decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects.

(3) That the information provided under Article 15(1)(h) must enable the data subject to exercise meaningfully their procedural rights to obtain human intervention, express their point of view and contest the decision. 
The case originated in a data subject’s request to understand the credit score generated by Dun & Bradstreet, a company specialising in credit assessment. Although the judgment concerns credit scoring, its implications extend to other domains, including employment, in which ADM continues to operate somewhat away from the light.

This Technical Brief provides a legal commentary on the Dun & Bradstreet Austria judgment, situating it above and beyond the scope of the GDPR and the AI Act. It examines its implications for algorithmic management and argues that the judgment establishes a systematic logic that must be applied in other fields, including in existing or upcoming legislation, given its reinforcement of workers’ rights under the GDPR. The Brief also proposes ways to operationalise the principles of the judgment in the employment context through complementary audit mechanisms inspired by certain provisions in the Digital Services Act.

title: Losing Ground: How Class Decline Fuels Far-Right Party Support in Europe
affiliations: University of Reading - School of Sociology, Politics and International Relations, University of Oslo and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - European Institute

detail.title: Losing Ground: How Class Decline Fuels Far-Right Party Support in Europe

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Key findings• Persons experiencing downward class mobility from the upper to the working class are more likely to support far-right parties. 

• This relationship is driven primarily by existential and material factors, such as life dissatisfaction and job and income insecurity, rather than distrust of elites or anti-immigration attitudes.

• National class mobility levels also affect this relationship: downward mobility has a stronger impact in societies in which levels of class decline are low overall. 

• Despite their propensity to support the far right, downwardly mobile persons constitute a small proportion of the far-right electorate. This suggests that this social group is not one of the main success drivers of the far-right, and should rather be seen as part of the often larger set of voters with economic grievances that make it possible for far-right parties to broaden their electoral base beyond their core supporters.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether historical complicity with communist institutions shapes contemporary perceptions of corruption. Using individual-level data from the Life in Transition Survey across 19 post-communist countries, we test two hypotheses: that former Communist Party members perceive higher levels of corruption, and that this relationship extends intergenerationally to the children of party members. The empirical results provide robust support for both propositions. Former party members exhibit significantly elevated corruption perceptions, an effect that persists across specifications controlling for historical legacies, economic development, and regime intensity. Children of party members display even stronger effects, suggesting that informal institutional norms are transmitted through household socialization. Countries that experienced more severe Stalinist rule show substantially higher corruption perceptions, indicating a dose-response relationship between repression intensity and institutional entrenchment. These findings demonstrate that corruption in post-communist societies reflects durable informal institutions reproduced across generations rather than merely contemporary incentive structures.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between inflation and GDP growth forecast errors and the expected monetary policy stance in the euro area during the monetary policy cycle of 2022-2024, when inflation was well above the ECB’s target. Under rational expectations, forecasts of monetary contractions should be unrelated to subsequent inflation and growth forecast errors. On the contrary, we find that expected monetary policy tightening has been associated with higher than projected GDP growth, suggesting a lower monetary policy effect than that factored in by (ECB/Eurosystem and IMF) forecasters. In other words, forecasters overestimated the monetary multiplier. At the same time, monetary policy tightening has been associated with lower than expected inflation, suggesting an underestimation of the monetary multiplier on inflation. Putting these two stylized facts together implies that forecasters overestimated the sacrifice ratio during the last monetary policy tightening cycle. Our findings suggest that forecasters may have inaccurately perceived the recent inflationary crisis in the euro area as predominantly supply-driven, underestimating its demand-driven component. This led to the belief that monetary policy in the euro area would be exceedingly costly in terms of output.

detail.abstract: We revisit the economic effects of marriage, analysing its heterogeneous impact on the intra-household labour division following childbirth. Can marriage promote coordination of work and child activities between parents and a gender egalitarian division of labour? Using a marginal treatment effect framework, we find the average effect of marriage is to increase parental specialization and worsen the mother's child penalty. However, we find differences across couples with varying resistance to marriage. While traditional couples (low-resistance) exhibit increased specialization; in modern couples (high-resistance) fathers have an earnings penalty and take more paternity leave, suggesting more coordination and gender equality.

title: Labor Market Strength and Declining Community College Enrollment
affiliations: and Harvard University

detail.title: Labor Market Strength and Declining Community College Enrollment

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Declining U.S. college enrollments over the past 15 years have triggered questions about the health of the postsecondary sector. Using institution-level data, we make four points. First, such declines are driven not by the four-year sector but by two-year community colleges, which have apparently shrunk by over 30% since the peak of the Great Recession. Second, over one-third of this apparent decline is an artifact of some community colleges being reclassified as offering four-year degrees. Third, pre-Great Recession data shows a 1 percentage point increase in the local unemployment rate increases first-time community college enrollment by 2 percent, suggesting many students are on the margin between community college and job opportunities. For-profit college enrollments are similarly countercyclical, while public and private four-year college enrollments appear acyclical. Our estimates suggest that strengthening labor markets explain about 60% of the post-Great Recession decline in first-time community college enrollment. Fourth, students whose enrollment decisions are most sensitive to labor market conditions appear unlikely to have completed a degree. Though declining community college enrollments are a challenge for postsecondary institutions, it is less clear whether they signal a problem for students on the margin of enrollment.

title: A Dynamic DCA-Leverage Algorithm for Optimized Average Positioning and Reduced Liquidation Risk

detail.title: A Dynamic DCA-Leverage Algorithm for Optimized Average Positioning and Reduced Liquidation Risk
detail.abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic DCA (Dollar Cost Averaging) combined with leverage allocation algorithm designed to optimize average entry pricing and reduce liquidation risk in volatile markets. The algorithm defines DCA points based on a controlled drawdown function: D k =f + k ((n+1)⋅2-f) n , k =0 , 1 ,2 , … , n where f represents the initial DCA percentage, n the total number of DCA entries, and k the DCA step index. By combining this DCA schedule with an increasing leverage sequence (e.g., 2x, 4x, 6x, 7x, 10x), the approach ensures that larger positions are taken at lower prices, improving average entry and overall risk management. Simulated scenarios demonstrate that increasing leverage produces superior average entry prices, maintains a safer liquidation buffer, and effectively scales invested amounts to maximize gains. Comparative analysis shows that decreasing or uniform leverage sequences result in higher average entry prices and higher liquidation risk. This research provides a systematic framework for traders seeking to combine DCA with leverage efficiently.

detail.title: Effects of Collateral Law Reform on Firms' Access to Finance
detail.abstract: It is widely believed that informational frictions coupled with limited abilities of small and medium entrepreneurs to put up collateral reduces allocative efficiency of financial markets in the developing countries. In recent years, initiatives have been put into motion to reform collateral laws in a number of countries. The main objective of these reforms is to relax financing constraints facing smaller firms by enabling them to use hitherto unused movable and intangible assets as collateral. Using firm level survey data from 88 developing countries for the period 2001-2011, the analysis seeks to examine the effects of such reforms on firms' perception about their access to credit. The results suggest that collateral reforms are effective in improving perceived access to credit only when they are accompanied by established collateral registries for movable and intangible assets. Furthermore, the perceived benefit of collateral reforms increases significantly with the firm size. This raises possibility that the effects of reforms are misaligned with its main objective of helping smaller firms.

detail.title: Interim Strategy-Proof Mechanisms

detail.abstract: Interim strategy-proofness (ISP) is a mechanism design criterion that extends strategyproofness to environments with interdependent values. It requires that each agent have an interim dominant strategy-one that is optimal against any strategies of others, given her beliefs about their types. We characterize ISP mechanisms for binary collective choices without transfers: a mechanism is ISP if and only if it satisfies Ordinality, Monotonicity, and a novel condition, Limited Outcome Externality (LOE). LOE bounds how much an agent's impact on the outcome can vary with others' actions, with the permissible variation inversely related to the magnitude of informational externalities faced by her in the environment. We apply the characterization to the jury model and identify optimal ISP voting rules. Under ISP, a weak Condorcet Jury Theorem holds, whereas the strong version fails.

title: Impact and cost-effectiveness of maternal vaccine and short and long-acting monoclonal antibodies against Respiratory Syncytial virus among infants in Japan: a modelling study

detail.title: Impact and cost-effectiveness of maternal vaccine and short and long-acting monoclonal antibodies against Respiratory Syncytial virus among infants in Japan: a modelling study
detail.abstract: Background: RSV infection is one of the most common causes of lower respiratory infection in Japan and globally. Three prevention measures — short-acting monoclonal antibody (sa-mAb) and long-acting monoclonal antibody (la-mAb) for infants, and RSV prefusion F protein vaccine (maternal vaccine (MV)) for pregnant women — are approved for use in Japan. We conducted cost-effectiveness analyses to inform intervention strategies to lower RSV disease burden among infants in Japan. Methods: We assessed the cost-effectiveness of six strategies for preventing RSV infection in comparison to no intervention; (i) sa-mAb for high-risk infants, (ii) MV for all pregnant women, (iii) la-mAb for high-risk infants,  (iv) la-mAb seasonal administration to all infants who were born between September and March, (v) la-mAb seasonal administration with catch-up administration in September for infants who were born between April and August, and (vi) la-mAb year-round administration to all infants. We also assessed the cost-effectiveness of MV combined with mAb for high-risk infants in comparison to MV-only. We conducted threshold analyses to identify the maximum price of MV and la-mAb at which they are cost-effective. Results: We estimated the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) for the maternal vaccine at JPY 6.7 million per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained, which exceeded the willingness-to-pay threshold in Japan of JPY 5 million per QALY gained. For la-mAb, the most cost-effective strategy was seasonal administration, although the ICER was over 180 million JPY per QALY gained with the current market price. A combination strategy of MV and mAb for high-risk infants was not cost-effective regardless of the prices of mAb. We estimated the threshold prices of MV at JPY 17,251 and la-mAb at JPY 11,443 –14,143. Conclusion: Among the RSV preventive interventions, MV was closest to being cost-effective. However, the price would have to be lowered for it to be cost-effective in Japan.

detail.abstract: Relevance. As interregional competition intensifies, state support for innovation in regional economies becomes increasingly important. To improve the effectiveness of such support, it is necessary to gain a better understanding of the link between innovation and economic development. Research Objective. The study aims to assess the impact of innovation activity on regional economic growth, focusing on the case of a large industrial region in Russia. Data and Methods. The analysis uses socioeconomic data for Sverdlovsk region from 2000 to 2023 and applies an autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) model to assess the relationship between innovation and economic performance. The study introduces an Innovation Activity Index, which incorporates several key components, such as the number of research personnel, internal R&D expenditures, and other relevant indicators, for a more comprehensive evaluation. However, while innovation clearly has a positively influence on economic growth in the short term, its effects over medium-and long-term periods are less obvious, likely due to structural factors in the regional economy. Conclusion. The study proposes recommendations to enhance regional innovation support within the «smart specialization» framework, including backing innovation projects, developing a sustainable innovation ecosystem, and investing in human capital.

title: Dynamic Spatial Treatment Effects and Network Fragility: Theory and Evidence from the 2008 Financial Crisis
affiliations: University of Tokyo

detail.title: Dynamic Spatial Treatment Effects and Network Fragility: Theory and Evidence from the 2008 Financial Crisis
detail.abstract: The 2008 financial crisis exposed fundamental vulnerabilities in interconnected banking systems, yet existing frameworks fail to integrate spatial propagation with network contagion mechanisms. This paper develops a unified spatial-network framework to analyze systemic risk dynamics, revealing three critical findings that challenge conventional wisdom. First, banking consolidation paradoxically increased systemic fragility: while bank numbers declined 47.3 percent from 2007 to 2023, network fragility measured by algebraic connectivity rose 315.8 percent, demonstrating that interconnectedness intensity dominates institutional count. Second, financial contagion propagates globally with negligible spatial decay (boundary d* = 47,474 km), contrasting sharply with localized technology diffusion (d* = 69 km)—a scale difference of 688 times. Third, traditional difference-in-differences methods overestimate crisis impacts by 73.2 percent when ignoring network structure, producing severely biased policy assessments. Using bilateral exposure data from 156 institutions across 28 countries (2007-2023) and employing spectral analysis of network Laplacian operators combined with spatial difference-in-differences identification, we document that crisis effects amplified over time rather than dissipating, increasing fragility 68.4 percent above pre-crisis levels with persistent effects through 2023. The consolidation paradox exhibits near-perfect correlation (r = 0.97) between coupling strength and systemic vulnerability, validating theoretical predictions from continuous spatial dynamics. Policy simulations demonstrate network-targeted capital requirements achieve 11.3x amplification effects versus uniform regulations. These findings establish that accurate systemic risk assessment and macroprudential policy design require explicit incorporation of both spatial propagation and network topology.

title: Curricular Governmental Speech: Legal Doctrine in the Anti-CRT Law and Policy Debates

detail.title: Curricular Governmental Speech: Legal Doctrine in the Anti-CRT Law and Policy Debates
detail.abstract: In this Article, I argue that the Eighth Circuit begins to articulate a doctrine that frames curricula as governmental speech in the anti-Critical Race Theory (CRT) context. Through a detailed analysis of the court's reasoning, this Article surfaces curricular governmental speech doctrine as the Walls court outlines it. To draw attention to this doctrine, the Article begins with a brief overview of the case. It then turns to the culture wars that gave rise to the Walls case, before turning to the legal bounds that Walls articulates in establishing this doctrine. The Article does not attempt to offer a comprehensive view of this doctrine; after all, the court articulates its rationale under an abuse of discretion standard as it determines whether the lower court rightfully granted students a preliminary injunction. In doing so, the court, however, examines whether the students would succeed on the merits of their claim, namely, that the state cannot arbitrarily adopt an anti-CRT law to change the curricula, because it violates their right-to-receive information. The goal of the Article, thus, is to flesh out the court's initial articulation of the doctrine, surfacing the court's concerns with democratic erosion and the role of courts into what the Eighth Circuit deems political questions in education. In this sense, this Article offers a starting point of inquiry for further analysis. To that end, the discussion and conclusion outline several domains implicated in the analysis of curricular governmental speech doctrine and in the anti-CRT law and policy debates, more broadly. These issues would benefit from further doctrinal and empirical study.

detail.abstract: In a series of comments and working papers, Joseph Francis attempts to challenge our empirical tests of Karl Marx's citation patterns following the Russian Revolution of 1917. One of Francis's main arguments purports to find parallel citation patterns of German novelist Thomas Mann, which he then interprets as an invalidation of our results for Marx. detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now used for economic reasoning, but their implicit "prefer ences" are poorly understood. We study LLM preferences as revealed by their choices in simple allocation games and a jobsearch setting. Most models favor equal splits in dictatorstyle allocation games, consistent with inequality aversion. Structural estimates recover FehrSchmidt parameters that indicate inequality aversion is stronger than in similar experiments with human participants. However, we find these preferences are malleable: reframing (e.g., masking social context) and learned control vectors shift choices toward payoffmaximizing behavior, while personas move them less effectively. We then turn to a more complex economic scenario. Extending a McCall job search environment, we also recover effective discounting from accept/ reject policies, but observe that model responses may not always be rationalizable, and in some cases suggest inconsistent preferences. Efforts to steer LLM responses in the McCall scenario are also less consistent. Together, our results suggest (i) LLMs exhibit latent preferences that may not perfectly align with typical human preferences and (ii) LLMs can be steered toward desired preferences, though this is more difficult with complex economic tasks.

detail.abstract: This paper uses text data from FOMC meeting transcripts to estimate the reference levels of full employment, inflation, and financial conditions perceived by voting members, and to uncover time variation in the Taylor rule parameters. We construct topic dictionaries on economic slack, inflation, and financial markets, and infer reference levels from members' sentiment using a statespace model. The estimated employment reference level indicates that FOMC voting members generally perceived the labor market as tighter than implied by the CBO's estimates between the mid-1980s and early 2000s, whereas the two measures align closely during the Great Recession and its subsequent recovery. The perceived inflation target varies widely in the 1970s and 1980s, trends downward in the 1990s, and stabilizes slightly below two percent thereafter. The estimated Taylor rule exhibits shifting policy weights over time-stronger emphasis on inflation stabilization before the mid-1990s, greater responsiveness to employment deviations thereafter, and renewed emphasis on the inflation trend following the Great Recession-while interest-rate smoothing remains substantial throughout.

detail.abstract: Solid waste management remains a serious global environmental problem, further exacerbated by rapid urbanization, increasing population growth, and consumption patterns in developing countries like the Philippines. detail.abstract: The Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations’ International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (Plant Treaty) provides that Farmers’ Rights includes the protection of traditional knowledge relevant to plant genetic resources for food and agriculture. This agreement is in harmony with the United Nations Environment Program’ Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) that has evolved and expanded with more international law about the traditional knowledge of Indigenous Peoples and local communities, recently establishing a Subsidiary Body on Article 8(j) and Other Provisions of the Convention Related to Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (SB8J) to replace the Ad Hoc Open-ended Working Group on Article 8(j) and Related Provisions of the Convention. This paper surveys the international scope of traditional knowledge as a foundation for developing the specific traditional knowledge obligations for Farmers’ Rights. The key points of controversy are addressed: identity and appropriate terminology; the sources of the traditional knowledge obligations; the scope of commitments under the CBD and Plant Treaty; the likely content of traditional knowledge; the requirements for legal pluralism; and the complexity from the contributions of different knowledge systems. The paper concludes with suggestions for future resolution: (1) adopting the appropriate terminology and distinguishing between the different groupings of Indigenous Peoples, local communities and farmers, perhaps recognising these overlapping groupings and that their legal interests in traditional knowledge linked to culture, land and territorial rights and governance systems may not be the same; (2) conceptualising the traditional knowledge relevant to plant genetic resources for food and agriculture so that it might be protected; (3) conceptualising legal mechanisms about co-existing legal orders (deep (true) legal pluralism); and (4) resolving the problems for assessing contributions and particularly shared traditional knowledge.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel methodological framework that employs solid bodies as threedimensional analytical instruments for the study of economic phenomena. Departing from traditional two-dimensional representations such as curves, surfaces, and equilibrium lines, this approach transforms economic relationships into volumetric geometric structures capable of capturing temporal dynamics, multidimensional interactions, structural shifts, and nonlinear behaviour. Solid bodies provide a richer and more comprehensive visualization of macroeconomic and microeconomic systems, enabling researchers to analyse stability regions, shock propagation, distortions, and the evolution of variables across time and space. By integrating this methodology with Econographicology, at the same time, the research paper demonstrates how solid structures including the Solid Phillips Surface Prototype (SPSP) offer deeper insights into complex economic processes. The use of solid bodies thus establishes a new paradigm in economic analysis, enhancing theoretical rigor, empirical interpretation, and pedagogical clarity across a wide range of economic applications.

detail.abstract:
Republic Act 9003 is a national law that introduces a complete and organized system for managing solid waste in the Philippines. It encourages reducing waste from the source, practicing proper segregation, recycling, composting, and using safe methods for waste disposal. The law requires households, barangays, and local government units (LGUs) to sort waste into biodegradable, non-biodegradable, recyclable, and special categories.

The act also calls for the creation of Solid Waste Management Boards at both national and local levels to guide the planning, implementation, and monitoring of waste management programs. LGUs must develop 10-year Solid Waste Management Plans, and barangays or groups of barangays are encouraged to set up Materials Recovery Facilities (MRFs). RA 9003 bans the use of open dumpsites and demands their closure or upgrading into controlled disposal facilities, eventually leading to the use of sanitary landfills. It also identifies the responsibilities of government offices, private sectors, and the public in promoting waste reduction and environmental protection.

In essence, RA 9003 highlights the importance of shared responsibility, community involvement, and sustainable practices to lessen the environmental and health problems caused by improper waste management.

detail.title: Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts via Soft Decision Tree Routing and Additive Networks
detail.abstract: We propose an Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts (IMoE) model that integrates soft decision tree routing with Neural Additive Models (NAMs) as experts. This architecture enables input-dependent expert specialization. At the same time, it preserves global transparency through additive feature decompositions and structured, axis-aligned routing. The model is trained end-to-end using a multi-phase optimization schedule that transitions from soft probabilistic routing to sparse and rule-based grouping. Empirically, the IMoE achieves predictive accuracy competitive with state-ofthe-art methods on two real-world tasks: credit scoring and insurance frequency modeling. Yet, the model offers richer economic interpretation than existing additive or black-box models. Our results demonstrate that modular, interpretable architectures can capture complex economic heterogeneity without sacrificing transparency or performance.

title: Arbitrator Selection Default Rules

detail.title: Arbitrator Selection Default Rules
detail.abstract:
This Article makes the case for changing the default settings for the selection of arbitrators in international commercial arbitration. For three-member tribunals, the rules of most international arbitration institutions provide that each party picks an arbitrator. The institution or the co-arbitrators then select the tribunal’s president. This prescription, which parties may set aside by agreement, codifies longstanding practices and corresponds to the strong preference of international arbitration insiders. Nonetheless, I argue that arbitration rules should default toward institutional selection of all arbitrators.

Switching the default nudges parties that can’t take full advantage of the arbitrator selection game—due to inexperience, lack of resources, or geography—toward a fairer arbitration process. Institutional selection of the entire tribunal reduces opportunities for insider parties to exploit selection and affiliation biases. Additionally, a setting in favor of institutional selection operates as a “penalty default.” It forces experienced parties to disclose their preference for party nomination and puts disadvantaged parties on inquiry notice about the tricky nature of arbitrator selection. There are also systemic reasons for making the switch, as institutions can use the increase in institutional appointments to improve representational balance. At the same time, transaction costs for opting out are low.

The proposed change to the choice architecture of arbitrator selection thus increases fairness in individual cases and promotes the longer-term legitimacy of international arbitration without sacrificing party autonomy.

detail.abstract: Traditional "checklist" definitions of life, based on Earth's biological characteristics, are facing a fundamental crisis in the frontiers of synthetic biology, artificial intelligence, and the search for extraterrestrial life. This paper proposes a radical paradigm shift: life is asystem that autonomously maintains and extends low entropy at both the material and informational levels. To validate the universality and explanatory power of this definition, we construct a"micro-empirical – macro-analogical – negative verification" framework: At the microscopic scale, the DishBrain experiment in vitro demonstrates that pure information processing is sufficient to drive autonomous learning and the emergence off unctional order (low entropy). At the macroscopic scale, we interpret the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) asa"macro-life" system that achieves socio-economic and geographical low-entropy expansion through energy metabolism and the production of public knowledge. Most convincingly, this framework is successfully applied to dissect the Russia-Ukraine conflict, revealing its essence as a fundamental collision between two competitive" macro-life" systems defending their mutually exclusive foundations of public knowledge(i.e., their core low-entropy orders). Finally, we outline a stratified pathway for the scientification and computability of this framework. We propose using energy flow to uniformly measure physical negative entropy(e.g., the "Civilization Energy Equivalent" metric) and using the intensity and complexity of public knowledge to measure informational negative entropy, aiming to integrate the minto a computable "Aliveness Index." This pathway will give rise to a new predictive science—Computational Aliveness—providing a unified theoretical foundation and diagnostic tool for understanding life phenomena, from viruses and AI to the rise and fall of civilizations.

title: Speech Is Only Free for the Privileged: The Moral Mechanics of Neutrality

detail.title: Speech Is Only Free for the Privileged: The Moral Mechanics of Neutrality
detail.abstract: This Article argues that the integrity of the First Amendment's promise of free expression depends less on the right to speak than on the discipline to translate speech into neutral, verifiable judgment. Freedom endures only when institutions-and the citizens who animate them-resist the cancel culture impulse to annex expression as truth before restating it in rule-governed terms. When emotion, faith, or reputation are usurped as authority without interpretation, neutrality collapses and speech becomes a form of orthodoxy. In such a system, hypocrisy is not a side effect-it is a structural inevitability. When authority is adopted without translation, free speech becomes a privilege of the elect, not a right of the governed. Drawing from case studies in law, religion, politics, and media-including Marsh v. Marsh, the SEC concealment scheme of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and the controversies surrounding Jimmy Kimmel and Representative Maxine Waters-this Article introduces a free speech translation principle (hereinafter Marsh Doctrine). The Marsh Doctrine holds that expressive acts must be translated before they can acquire institutional consequence. Translation preserves contestability; adoption erases it. A society that translates before it reacts remains both free and self-governing.

title: Dispatch or Hold? An Inverse Optimization and Reinforcement Learning Approach for Multi-Objective On-Demand Delivery

detail.title: Dispatch or Hold? An Inverse Optimization and Reinforcement Learning Approach for Multi-Objective On-Demand Delivery
detail.abstract: Problem definition: In large-scale on-demand food delivery systems, dynamic order dispatching needs to balance immediate dispatch and order holding amid competing objectives-including delivery efficiency, service timeliness, and courier utilization. Holding certain orders for future consolidation may improve delivery efficiency but impair timeliness. In such systems, real-time decisions must be made to determine both when to dispatch orders and how to dispatch orders by grouping them to share dispatch routes. Methodology/results: We propose a hierarchical offline estimation and on-policy learning framework that integrates inverse optimization with deep reinforcement learning. First, the framework decides which orders to dispatch immediately and which to hold for future periods. Next, it consolidates the dispatched orders by solving a multi-objective weighted set partitioning problem. We estimate the trade-off weights across multiple delivery objectives using real-world data via cutting-plane-based inverse optimization that supports combinatorial decisions. The learned cost structure is then embedded in a Markov decision process, and a dispatch policy is trained with Proximal Policy Optimization to maximize long-term performance. We validate our approach using real-world data from a major food delivery platform. Compared to the platform's current practice and the heuristic benchmarks, the learned policy significantly improves operational performance and provides the most effective balance across all operational objectives. Implications: The evaluation results demonstrate that strategic order holding can effectively increase grouping opportunities and improve overall delivery efficiency. In periods and areas with low order arrival density, a longer holding time can yield better consolidation opportunities and improved delivery efficiency. However, orders with long travel distances are less suitable for holding due to limited potential for grouping.

detail.title: Predicting Seasonal Variations of River Water Quality: An Artificial Intelligence (AI) Approach Integrating Physicochemical Parameters
detail.abstract: Characterization and prediction of seasonal variations in river water quality are essential for keeping the control of aquatic ecosystems and resource management. This study aims to develop predictive models using Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques, particularly Machine Learning (ML) algorithms, to classify seasonal patterns in three major rivers in Bangladesh: Buriganga, Shitalakhya, and Turag. The study considered 15 of the most significant water quality parameters, including pH, alkalinity, biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), total dissolved solids (TDS), and electrical conductivity (EC). A total of 476 samples were gathered on a monthly basis at 17 monitoring points in the three rivers, covering all months between January and December from 2021 to 2023. With K-fold cross-validation and hyperparameter optimization, three ML models like Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest (RF), and Decision Tree (DT), were employed for predicting seasonal variation in river water quality. The models were assessed based on accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC–AUC scores. Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) analysis was applied to explore the marginal effects of key water quality features on seasonal prediction while keeping other variables constant. RF achieved the highest accuracy of 79%, and XGBoost was about 77% among the models. The SHAP analysis demonstrated TDS, Alkalinity and EC as the top feature drivers of seasonal differences, providing insight into the interplay between chemical composition and climate. The results of the study have the potential to accurately depict the seasonal patterns in river water quality using AI approaches.

detail.abstract: We leverage a fire outbreak that caused a large but temporary capacity loss at the largest US beef packer to study how firm conduct shapes the pass-through of supply disruptions along the supply chain. detail.abstract:
This policy paper provides a comprehensive analysis of Germany's 2025 pension reform package (Rentenpaket 2025), based on legislative draft 21/1929. The reform guarantees a pension level of 48% until 2031 and introduces a €200 billion "Generational Capital Fund" (Generationenkapital) – a capital market-based component intended to stabilize contribution rates. Through detailed financial modeling, scenario analysis, and generational equity calculations, this study demonstrates that the reform constitutes a costly palliative measure rather than a structural solution to demographic pressures.

Key findings include: (1) The pension level guarantee generates annual costs exceeding €13 billion by 2040; (2) The Generational Capital Fund yields only 0.4 percentage points of contribution rate relief – effectively negligible; (3) Younger cohorts (born 2000) face a negative real return of -21.9%, compared to +16.1% for baby boomers (born 1960); (4) Contribution rates will rise from 18.6% (2025) to 21.2% (2040), imposing €54 billion in additional annual costs on the economy.

The analysis evaluates seven alternative reform options, identifying automatic pension age indexation to life expectancy (Danish/Swedish model) as the most effective structural measure, capable of reducing contribution rates by 2.5 percentage points and saving €15-20 billion annually. The paper concludes that without fundamental reforms – including pension age adjustments, incorporation of civil servants, and reinstatement of the sustainability factor – Germany's pension system will impose unsustainable fiscal burdens on future generations.

detail.title: CSR Reporting of Private Firms
detail.abstract: In this study, we investigate the quantity and quality of private firms' CSR reporting. Using textual analysis of annual reports and websites from a representative random sample of all German private firms, we identify and classify CSR-related sentences. We find that CSR-related disclosures account for approximately 7% of sentences in annual reports and websites. Moreover, private firms primarily disclose social-related CSR topics in their annual reports, particularly focusing on employees, with websites covering a broader range of social topics. By contrast, environmental topicssuch as climate changeare less frequently reported in either channel. Quantitative or specific CSR information is limited in both disclosure channels, while standardized communication, such as the stickiness of prior years' documents, is significantly more prevalent than for non-CSR information. Finally, we find that financial factors only play a minor role in explaining the quantity and quality of private firms' CSR reporting. Instead, contextual factors, such as supply chain structures, competitive intensity, and the presence of public firms, appear to be more influential.

detail.abstract: We study how hate speech affects prosocial behavior in a laboratory setting. detail.title: A Simplified Thermal Model with Robust Extrapolation Performance for Cooling Towers
detail.abstract: This study presents a simplified thermal model with high prediction accuracy and robust extrapolation performance for cooling tower control optimization. The model modifies the effectiveness-NTU model by incorporating empirical expressions derived from detailed analyzes of heat and mass transfer processes in cooling towers and the thermodynamic properties of moist air. The model has an explicit formulation with four bounded parameters that can be identified using measurement data. The prediction performance of the proposed model was thoroughly evaluated and compared with five known gray-box models using operating data from a counter-flow cooling tower system. The dataset spans a broad operational range, offering an ideal basis for analyzes. The results demonstrate that the proposed model is the only model that consistently meets the accuracy thresholds in all comparative analyzes. It also exhibits robust extrapolation performance, maintaining high accuracy under unseen conditions, regardless of whether the training dataset is diverse or limited in range. These qualities make the proposed model well-suited for real-time control optimization of cooling tower systems, particularly for newly installed systems with limited data availability due to time constraints, and for systems in mission-critical facilities, such as data centers, where operational limitations restrict the data range.

title: AI-First from the Employee Perspective: Evidence-Based Guide to Adoption

detail.title: AI-First from the Employee Perspective: Evidence-Based Guide to Adoption
detail.abstract:
Abstract: Organizations worldwide are mandating "AI-first" approaches, yet a massive disconnect exists: while 66% of employees use AI tools regularly, only 46% trust them and a mere 6% feel comfortable doing so. This research synthesizes evidence from 50+ peer-reviewed studies (2018-2025), official frameworks (NIST AI RMF, OECD AI Principles, EU AI Act), and documented implementation failures to explain this adoption crisis.

Three critical findings emerge: First, AI creates a "jagged technological frontier"—boosting productivity by 66% on average within capability boundaries but causing 19-percentage-point performance drops outside them. Experts cannot reliably identify these boundaries. Second, AI adoption triggers psychological damage through a mediation pathway: reducing psychological safety (β=-0.324, p<0.001) which increases employee depression (β=-0.211, p<0.001). Third, a dangerous training gap exists—75% of companies deploy AI but only 35% train employees, creating predictable failures documented at Samsung, Ring, and Clearview AI.

This paper provides actionable frameworks validated through empirical research: (1) Starter and Level-Up playbooks addressing different expertise levels, (2) validated measurement instruments (MAILS, AILS, GAIL) for tracking adoption, (3) evidence-based counters to four systematic pitfalls, and (4) ethical guardrails for privacy, bias, and compliance. The research reveals successful patterns—"centaurs" (clear human-AI division) and "cyborgs" (continuous integration)—while demonstrating that "AI-first" cannot mean "AI-only."

Practical implications span individual employees navigating adoption anxiety, managers implementing AI without destroying team morale, and organizations seeking productivity gains without legal liability or workforce alienation.

detail.abstract: A synthesis of family works is always welcome; properly speaking, the family can be written indefinitely, given the very diversified range of values under which it can be studied. It is unanimously accepted that belonging to a family makes the survival of the individual as a social being and the reproduction of society possible. A series of social changes, among which the liberalization of family life, disturbed the stability conferred by the family system and produced changes in the form, structure and family relations. A closer analysis on how the family can be described justifies Stolnici’s (2015, p.7) statement that the family is approached today as a process rather than as an institution, more as fluidity than as structure. Family life seems to flow, always in commitments and plans for the future, always involved in projects and responsibilities. We are more chal-lenged than ever to respond to personal, professional, contextual, economic, etc. requirements, which are increasingly complex and diversified. The family as a system, therefore, sums up several individuals, more and more frequently dis-connected from each other, involved in separate lives, different experiences. The complexity of life has become more and more overwhelming. We are involved, so each of us in a continuous process of development, training, adaptation to the environment, discovery and rediscovery of internal resources for a permanent self-actualization. Studies on the family include, perhaps, the richest and most diverse approaches, being frequently related to the subject of dysfunctions or so-cial problems. Constituting the central element of the socio-economic system, the family has been the target over time of countless changes and pressures that have shaped and transposed it into an ever-changing reality, to which it has adapted differently, depending on the cultural specifics.

detail.abstract: As hospital systems consolidate and negotiate higher private health insurance (PHI) reimbursements, the widening difference between PHI and public hospital payments could incentivize hospitals to restrict access to care for lower-margin Medicaid beneficiaries. We examine how hospital mergers affect labor and delivery (L&D) care for mothers covered by Medicaid. Using national Medicaid claims data and US vital statistics data, we find that Medicaid birth admissions decline by an average of 29% following a within-market hospital merger. This reduction is largely attributed to a corresponding 12% decrease in the number of unique L&D providers at merged facilities. Rates of cesarean delivery show modest declines, with no measurable change in induced labor rates. At the county level, newborn health outcomes improve in areas served by hospitals that acquire other facilities. Overall, hospital consolidation appears to reduce access to within-market hospital options while yielding modest improvements in birth outcomes for mothers admitted for L&D care.

The EAC, with its flagship application in Rent-to-Own (RTO), operates on a transparent, tripartite ledger system that algorithmically allocates periodic payments into consumption, equity, and cost components. We present a complete mathematical specification and a disciplined operational workflow designed for global applicability. Utilizing the NestQuestROI simulation engine and extensive, publicly available United States historical data (1971 – 2023)—selected for its depth and longitudinal authenticity—we demonstrate that the EAC structure offers a compelling risk-return profile for both sponsors and users. The data shows that the EAC can outperform traditional rental models on key metrics like Real Net Operating Margin (RNOM) for sponsors and provide a positive real return for occupant-buyers where renting offers none. Crucially, this framework is universal; its core mathematics remain constant, but its legal and parametric implementation must be meticulously calibrated to 100% comply with local laws, using the host jurisdiction's real estate, tenancy, and financial regulations as its governing framework. This work establishes the EAC as a quantitatively validated, accounting-transparent model for achieving greater stability and returns, with the explicit understanding that its successful deployment hinges on local legal obedience and parametric customization.

detail.title: Federal Control of State Structure

contentType.other: already selected, forthcoming law journal article

detail.abstract:
The conventional narrative holds that the federal Constitution mandates a tripartite separation of powers at the federal level but says nothing about state government structure. States, rather, have free rein to organize themselves as they wish.

This Article challenges the conventional narrative as reductive and largely wrong. True, no constitutional provision explicitly controls state structure. The closest is the Republican Guarantee Clause, which has not been understood to control state structure in any enforceable way.

Yet as this Article catalogues, several other federal constitutional provisions and doctrines have the effect of controlling state structure. Rooted in the enforcement of federal individual-rights guarantees, these doctrines are not necessarily about state structure. But they all have the collateral consequence of requiring states to separate either legislative power from non-legislative power, executive power from non-executive power, or judicial power from non-judicial power.

Considered all together, these various doctrines require, as a matter of federal constitutional law, that states maintain a tripartite separation of powers. They also set forth standards for policing the required separation in accordance with federal law. And, because they ultimately derive from individual-rights guarantees, they are judicially enforceable.

In sum, this Article constructs a theory of federal control of state structure based on existing constitutional doctrines. In addition to exposing the conventional narrative of federal–state interaction as (at best) incomplete, the theory also has further implications. For one, it may help explain perceived tensions between modern structure-controlling doctrines, on the one hand, and constitutional history, on the other. It may also suggest a gravitational-pull reading of the Republican Guarantee Clause that preserves a role for that Clause in constitutional discourse, even if not in constitutional adjudication. And it may offer a useful, theoretically grounded way of interpreting and applying Moore v. Harper’s reference to “ordinary judicial review” in the election-law context.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nil.

detail.abstract:
Background
On 19 November 2025 the New Zealand Government used the Medicines Act 1981 to restrict puberty blockers (GnRHa) for transgender adolescents. Framed as a "precautionary approach," the decision created a higher evidentiary standard for this group than is applied elsewhere in paediatric medicine.

Analysis
We argue that the ban is an instance of "Regulatory Exceptionalism." We analyse a 44-document policy corpus and extract a 32-field matrix from 12 core policy documents. This material is interpreted through a seven-pillar framework: demanding near-impossible evidence (Epistemological), misdiagnosing rising demand (Economic), bypassing normal processes (Procedural), suspending rights (Constitutional), weaponizing uncertainty (Discourse), inverting non-maleficence (Ethical), and using a health issue for political gain (Political Economy).

Conclusion
Comparing the ban with the routine off-label use of other medicines and the government's parallel push to deregulate medicine approvals shows this policy is an outlier. It reflects evidence selection shaped by policy preference, creating a differential standard of care for transgender youth.

We argue that the solution lies not in ending migration, but in resurrecting a universal principle of coexistence, perfectly captured by the Indonesian proverb "Dimana bumi dipijak, disitu langit dijunjung"—"Wherever you set your foot, there you uphold the sky." This is the non-negotiable duty to respect the local social contract, a concept that is the ultimate antidote to the corrosive forces of supremacist ideology and the key to a stable, pluralistic future.

title: A Dual Learning Model for Last-Mile Delivery Pricing

detail.title: A Dual Learning Model for Last-Mile Delivery Pricing
detail.abstract: Last-mile delivery platforms encounter significant order cancellations due to uncertainty about the customer's willingness to pay adequate delivery fee and also the driver's willingness to accept such offers. The current approach of using static pricing models fail to adapt to this dual uncertainty, leading to suboptimal market outcomes. This paper develops a framework to address this challenge by modeling this as a learning problem. We formulate the interaction as a stackelberg game where the platform acts as the leader, making direct price and payout offers. We propose and compare two learning methodologies for the platform: a model-based approach that simultaneously learns the parameters of customer and driver valuation functions using a gradient-based method, and a modelfree Q-learning approach that directly learns an optimal pricing policy. Numerical simulations demonstrate that both learning approaches significantly outperform a non-learning, fixed-rate benchmark policy. Both the model-based and model-free approaches are shown to converge towards the true underlying values over time, leading to more efficient transaction outcomes and a larger total economic surplus for the platform, customers, and drivers. The results highlight the substantial value of adaptive learning in such a two-sided market. By actively managing this exploration-exploitation trade-off, a platform can uncover latent market dynamics, automate its pricing strategy, and achieve superior long-term profitability. This provides a clear advantage over static pricing mechanisms.

detail.title: Youth Radicalization as a Regional Security Threat: Global South and Bangladesh Perspectives Author
detail.abstract:
Youth radicalization has emerged as a critical security challenge across many parts of the Global South, where demographic youth bulges, economic exclusion, political marginalization, and rapidly expanding digital connectivity interact to create fertile ground for extremist recruitment and mobilization. This paper examines youth radicalization as a multi-causal, socially embedded process and argues that its implications extend beyond individual trajectories to pose significant regional security threats—transnational recruitment, cross-border militant mobility, diaspora-mediated financing, and digital propaganda spillovers. Drawing on established theoretical models (e.g., Moghaddam’s ‘staircase to terrorism’), recent empirical studies, and policy reports focused on South Asia and Bangladesh, the paper synthesizes drivers (structural, ideological, social, and
technological), pathways (offline and online), and outcomes (violence, instability, and governance erosion). Bangladesh is used as a detailed case study: despite important counter-extremism gains in the 2010s, emergent socio-political crises, high youth unemployment, periodic mass protests, and intensified online information ecosystems have contributed to renewed vulnerability among segments of youth. The paper maps how local grievances are sometimes reframed by transnational
extremist narratives and how social media accelerates radical socialization, while state responses (security operations, closure of civic space) both mitigate and, at times, exacerbate drivers by alienating communities. Policy implications emphasize a regional, multi-level approach: (1) socioeconomic inclusion and youth employment; (2) community-led prevention and resilience; (3) calibrated law enforcement aligned with human rights; (4) digital literacy and platform accountability; and (5) enhanced cross-border cooperation for intelligence, deradicalization, and reintegration. The conclusion calls for research-policy partnerships in the Global South to design context-sensitive CVE (countering violent extremism) strategies and recommends longitudinal evaluation of prevention interventions to reduce risk while preserving civic freedoms.

detail.title: Remedy or Retreat? Investigating Ex-post Incentives under the One-Vote Veto System
detail.abstract: This study offers a nuanced exploration of the unintended behavioral consequences stemming from the one-vote veto system---a performance evaluation mechanism that nullifies all achievements in the event of a critical failure. While previous research has largely concentrated on the ex-ante effects of such systems---how they shape agents' efforts to avoid failures---this paper shifts focus to the ex-post strategic responses of agents, particularly local government officials in China, following veto-triggering events like major workplace safety accidents (WSAs). Using a comprehensive prefecture-by-day dataset on WSAs and employing a regression discontinuity design in time, with the dates of major WSAs as the cutoff, we uncover significant behavioral shifts. Before the implementation of the veto system, local governments actively engaged in remedial actions after WSAs, such as intensifying efforts to promote economic growth and environmental protection. However, following the introduction of the veto system, these compensatory measures ceased, indicating that local officials abandoned broader efforts once a single failure nullified all other accomplishments. Further analysis reveals that this behavioral shift is closely linked to promotion incentives, as the rigid accountability framework diminished the motivation to address failures holistically. By shedding light on the adverse effects of the one-vote veto system, this study provides critical insights for policymakers aiming to design effective performance evaluation systems, especially in contexts where overly rigid mechanisms risk undermining comprehensive governance and sustained effort.

detail.abstract: The onset of the coronavirus has catalyzed an acceleration in the adoption of digital teaching practices that have been trending in Higher Education for over a decade. The most obvious of these has been the abrupt switch to online training. Given the speed at which this transition from in-person instruction has taken place, many instructors' natural first inclination has been to maintain teaching styles as similar as possible to those employed in person, including the traditional lecture format. However, a growing body of research is confirming what instructors across the educational spectrum are observing: namely, that student behaviour, the psychological effect of the medium, participation levels, attention span and learning outcomes online can vary widely from those demonstrated in traditional classroom settings. It is becoming increasingly clear that conditions such as "Zoom fatigue" are very real, and that, if teaching is to be effective, different methodologies based on digital learning experiences should be added to educators' repertoires that take the particular challenges and new opportunities of the online environment into consideration. This paper will examine how some of these new online-based methodologies and digital tools are being developed and introduced at the University of Europe within the undergraduate students' Employability module to enhance the student online experience as well as learning outcomes. detail.title: Coffee-Based Agroforestry Systems as a Sustainable Forest Management Strategy: Evidence from Humbang Hasundutan, Indonesia
detail.abstract: Deforestation and land degradation remain pressing challenges in Indonesia, particularly in forest-margin areas where agricultural expansion drives ecological decline. Coffee-based agroforestry has emerged as a promising strategy to reconcile ecological conservation with socio-economic development. This study analyzes the characteristics, ecological functions, and economic contributions of coffee-based agroforestry systems in Humbang Hasundutan Regency, North Sumatra, Indonesia. Using a mixed-methods approach, primary data were collected through field surveys, soil and vegetation analysis, and farmer interviews, complemented by secondary spatial and statistical datasets. The study applied land suitability analysis, economic feasibility assessment, and modeling of biomass and carbon stocks to evaluate system performance across different forest types and management zones. Results indicate that coffee-based agroforestry systems significantly enhance land productivity and farmer income compared to monoculture practices, with average household earnings exceeding regional minimum living standards. Ecologically, these systems reduce soil erosion, improve soil fertility and water retention, and contribute to biodiversity conservation. Multistrata agroforestry models demonstrated higher carbon sequestration potential (up to 52 t C/ha) compared to simplified systems, highlighting their role in climate change mitigation. The integration of diverse shade trees not only stabilizes microclimatic conditions but also provides complementary products such as fruits, timber, and fuelwood, further diversifying farmer livelihoods. This study concludes that coffee-based agroforestry represents a viable alternative for sustainable forest management in tropical uplands. By integrating ecological, economic, and social dimensions, it offers a pathway to align local livelihoods with global sustainability targets, including SDG 15 on life on land. Policy support, capacity building, and long-term monitoring are essential to optimize system adoption and scalability across forest-margin communities.
